Constable, primarily a landscapist, treats her face with a reserved tenderness, the muted palette and soft modelling reflecting the private nature of the commission.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-a-bo: A barge being lowered through the lock at Flatford Mill on the Stour, the lock-keeper leaning on the beam against a clearing sky. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1824 and sold on opening day, the picture was the only one of Constable's six-footers to find a buyer during the artist's lifetime.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-bran: A pond on Hampstead Heath under a banked sky, with riders on the sandy track at the rim. Constable rented a house in Hampstead from 1819 to give his consumptive wife Maria cleaner air, and the heath supplied him with the open-sky subjects he returned to throughout the 1820s.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-by-r: The young John Constable, then twenty-three, faces the viewer in dark coat and stock, his curling hair brushed forward. Reinagle painted the portrait in 1799, the year both men entered the Royal Academy Schools, and it now hangs in the National Portrait Gallery in London.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-flat: A view from a footbridge on the Stour, with a barge being unhitched in the foreground beneath open Suffolk sky. Painted largely en plein air on Constable's family land, the picture exemplifies the truth-to-nature creed that underpinned his six large 'Stour' canvases.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-hadl: The ruined fourteenth-century keep of Hadleigh Castle stands on the Essex shore above the wide grey mouth of the Thames, gulls wheeling in a clearing morning sky. Constable submitted the picture to the Royal Academy in 1829, the year of his election as an Academician and shortly after the death of his wife Maria; it now belongs to the Yale Center for British Art.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-harw: A breezy view of the Essex coast, with the squat Low Lighthouse anchoring a beach where small figures gather under a luminous, cloud-stacked sky. Constable's skies are scientifically observed, drawing on his sustained study of meteorology in oil sketches.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-parh: A weatherboarded watermill at Gillingham in Dorset, its great wheel still and the mill pond catching a high English light. Constable exhibited the picture at the Royal Academy in 1826, working from drawings made on visits to his friend Archdeacon John Fisher; the building itself had burned down the year before he painted it.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-sali: The thirteenth-century spire of Salisbury Cathedral framed between tall trees in the Bishop's garden, cattle grazing at the edge of a sunlit meadow. Signed and dated 1826 and now in the Frick Collection, the picture was repainted by Constable at the request of Bishop John Fisher, who had objected to the dark sky of an earlier version.

The cathedral's spire rises through the screen of trees on a property owned by the painter's friend Bishop Fisher, who commissioned the picture. Constable renders the verdant grounds with characteristic flecks of white impasto — his 'snow' that animated foliage and water alike.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-sir-: A view from Haverstock Hill in rural Hampstead, looking south toward the dome of St Paul's, with Sir Richard Steele's cottage on the right and the Load of Hay inn on the left. Constable, who had lived in Hampstead since 1819, sketched the rise repeatedly; the cottage was demolished in 1867.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-ston: A late watercolour showing the prehistoric stones beneath a roiling sky split by a double rainbow. Constable, working in his final years, treats the monument as a meditation on time and weather, the broken trilithons set against the moving drama of the English heavens.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-the-: A wooden hay cart fords the millpond at Flatford on the Stour, with Willy Lott's cottage to the left and a slow bank of cumulus overhead. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1821, the six-foot canvas was shown at the 1824 Paris Salon, where it won a gold medal and influenced Delacroix and the young Barbizon painters.

A sweeping view east from Gun Hill over the River Stour to the tower of Dedham Church and the estuary beyond, painted with thickly worked impasto and white sparkle on the water. Dated 1828 and now in the Scottish National Gallery, the picture echoes Claude's Hagar and the Angel and helped secure Constable's election to the Royal Academy the following year.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-wate: Waterloo Bridge seen from the Whitehall stairs, its arches stretching across the Thames under a banked grey sky. Constable worked on the Waterloo subject for nearly two decades, building from this study toward the large 1832 picture commemorating the bridge's opening on the seventh anniversary of the battle.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-wive: A panoramic estate view commissioned by Major-General Francis Slater-Rebow, balancing fishermen, swans, a grazing herd, and the distant house. Constable expanded the canvas at the patron's request to include a lawn and outbuildings, evidence of his pragmatic handling of the country-house genre.
collection-of-beauty-john-everett-millai: Titled from a song in Shakespeare's As You Like It, the painting shows a young woman trudging through a bleak snowbound landscape. By the 1890s Millais had moved away from his early Pre-Raphaelite tightness toward a broader, more mood-driven late style.

An autumnal Perthshire backwater under leaden skies, painted from a sandbank on the Tay near Murthly. Millais himself called this his first true landscape, and its damp, unromantic mood anticipates the meditative late landscapes that occupied his final decades.

A snow-covered Scottish vista at twilight, the windows of a distant house glowing against winter blue. Millais's late landscapes increasingly dispense with figures and narrative, trading Pre-Raphaelite detail for atmospheric tonal painting in the manner of his hero Turner.

A view of the Perthshire glen near Dunkeld where Millais routinely summered and painted. The wet leaf-strewn ground and bare birches are handled with the freer, broader brushwork of his maturity, far from the meticulous botanical inventories of his Pre-Raphaelite youth.

Drawn from Tennyson's poem after the Shakespearean character, Mariana stretches wearily at her embroidery beside a stained-glass window, autumn leaves drifting onto the floor. Millais paints the heraldic glass and velvet gown with founding Pre-Raphaelite precision, every fibre and pane separately observed.

Shakespeare's drowning Ophelia drifts among meadow flowers along the Hogsmill River in Surrey. Millais painted the riverbank botany on site over five months, then posed Elizabeth Siddal in a heated bathtub for the figure. Each bloom carries Victorian floral symbolism for grief, innocence and madness.

A young Brunswick cavalry officer takes leave of his sweetheart on the eve of Waterloo, her hand braced against the door he is determined to open. Millais paired the black death's-head hussar uniform against shimmering ivory silk to heighten the parting. Charles Dickens's daughter Kate modelled for the woman.
collection-of-beauty-john-frederick-lewi: A young Egyptian woman carries a brass coffee tray through a marble courtyard, ducking below the lintel of a sunlit doorway. Lewis stages the scene to showcase the architectural light effects he studied during his Cairo years. The metalwork, sash and tilework are executed with miniaturist watercolour precision in oils.

A British traveller's tent camp pitched in the Sinai wilderness, with St Catherine's monastery faintly visible in the distance. Lewis drew on a decade of life in Cairo to render carpets, tasselled saddles and Bedouin retainers with miniaturist exactitude. The watercolour fuses Orientalist reportage with the topographical tradition.

A harem interior in Cairo, where a seated lady greets her guests amid mashrabiya screens and a sun-dappled mosaic floor. Lewis lived a decade in an Ottoman house in the city and made the filtered light through latticed windows his signature subject. Every textile, slipper and tile is rendered in jewel-bright watercolour clarity.

A late biblical genre piece taking its title from the Epistle of James, set within a sunlit Eastern interior. Lewis casts the scriptural episode in the Cairene domestic vocabulary he had perfected over decades. Mashrabiya light falls across patterned cushions and the bedside attendants in saturated colour.

An early Scottish genre piece from before Lewis's Mediterranean and Egyptian years, showing crofters welcoming visitors at a Highland hearth. The picture belongs to a brief vogue for Walter Scott-inflected tartan subjects shared with Landseer. Lewis already shows his appetite for textured plaids, deer carcasses and rough stone interiors.

A late riverside scene from Upper Egypt, with figures and pack animals drawn up on a sunlit bank above the Nile. Painted long after Lewis's return to England, it draws on the cache of Cairo sketchbooks he mined for the rest of his career. The high horizon and clear ochre palette typify his desert manner.

A group of Italian pilgrims rests on the road, products of Lewis's residence in Rome during the late 1830s before he settled in Cairo. The picture catalogues regional costume with the same ethnographic precision he would later turn on the Ottoman world. It marks his transition from Spanish to Mediterranean genre subjects.
collection-of-beauty-john-hancock-painti: John Hancock sits at a writing table in a blue coat with his ledger open before him, the merchant and future signer of the Declaration of Independence painted at twenty-eight. Copley made the portrait in 1765 for the Hancock family in Boston, and it now hangs in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-john-henry-newman-b: Cardinal Newman, leader of the Oxford Movement and convert to Rome, sits in scarlet biretta and mozzetta near the end of his life. Millais paints the theologian with the brisk, grand-manner brushwork of his late society portraiture. The picture was commissioned soon after Newman received the cardinal's hat from Leo XIII.
collection-of-beauty-john-jay-gilbert-st: John Jay sits in the black robes of the first Chief Justice of the United States, a closed book under his hand. Stuart began the portrait in London in 1794 while Jay was negotiating the treaty that bears his name, completing the canvas after his return; it is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-john-liston-byam-sh: A young woman in a dark dress stands lost in thought at the edge of an overgrown stream, the summer vegetation around her painted with Pre-Raphaelite exactness. The war of the title never appears: Byam Shaw shows only its cost at home, a woman mourning a loss in a conflict thousands of miles away, the indifferent lushness of the English countryside sharpening her grief. Painted in 1901 under the title The Boer War, the oil is in the collection of Birmingham Museums.

Eve panel from a triptych on the Fall, with Adam and the serpent occupying the flanking compartments. Byam Shaw extends the late Pre-Raphaelite manner of Burne-Jones and Rossetti into the Edwardian era, with hothouse colour and stylised vegetation. The figure is set against a tapestry of curling leaves and ripe fruit.
collection-of-beauty-john-singer-sargent: The painter Paul Helleu sketches outdoors beside his wife Alice, the canoe and grass rendered in broken Impressionist touch. Sargent painted the work at Fladbury during a summer of plein-air experiment under Monet's influence. The flushed greens and unfinished edges show him at his most explicitly Impressionist.

A circular ceiling painting for the rotunda of the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, showing the Titan stooping under the celestial sphere while the nymphs of the western garden recline at his feet. Sargent took on the rotunda decoration as a late, demanding mural commission. The composition reads from any vantage on the floor below.

Breton women and children file across the tidal flats of Cancale at low water, baskets balanced on shoulders. The Salon-scale picture established the twenty-two-year-old Sargent in Paris and won a second-class medal in 1878. The wet sand mirrors a high pearly sky in long horizontal bands of grey-blue.

Two girls in white pinafores light Japanese paper lanterns among carnations and tall lilies in a Cotswold garden at dusk. Sargent painted only in the brief twilight window each day across two summers in Broadway. The Tate canvas became the picture that rehabilitated his reputation in England after the Madame X scandal.

Gertrude Vernon, the new Lady Agnew, leans back in a bamboo chair in a white satin gown with a lavender sash, one hand draped loosely over the armrest. Sargent's commission for Sir Andrew Agnew was painted in six sittings during 1892 and shown at the Royal Academy in 1893; it now anchors the Scottish National Gallery.

A languid female figure reclines on a sofa, head turned away, wrapped in shimmering ivory satin and gauze. Sargent's niece Rose-Marie Ormond was the model for several such drapery studies in the years before the First World War. The picture is essentially a virtuoso exercise in painting white folds against deep shadow.

A personification of the defeated Synagogue, blindfolded and clutching a broken staff, painted for Sargent's Triumph of Religion mural cycle in the Boston Public Library. The medieval iconographic pairing with a triumphant Church drew sustained protest from Boston's Jewish community. The cycle was left unfinished, partly in the wake of that controversy.

Two friends bend over a board in a sun-shot garden during one of Sargent's Alpine summers in the Simplon. The painter spent these holidays sketching members of his travelling party in shawls, hats and Kashmiri textiles. The watercolour-like oil handling and high-keyed greens are typical of these informal late landscapes.

A street vendor stands in the cool gloom of a Venetian calle, a string of onions slung from her hand. The picture belongs to Sargent's early Venetian campaigns of 1880-82, when he prowled working-class quarters off the tourist routes. Tonal greys and a single shaft of light recall Velazquez, whom he had recently studied in Madrid.
collection-of-beauty-john-singleton-copl: British soldiers rally over the body of Major Francis Peirson after the French assault on Jersey in January 1781, the Union flag advancing through the smoke of the market square at St Helier. Copley's 1783 history painting, commissioned by the print publisher John Boydell, hangs in Tate Britain.

Admiral Duncan receives the sword of the defeated Vice-Admiral de Winter on the quarterdeck of HMS Venerable after the British victory off Camperdown on 11 October 1797. Copley finished the canvas in 1799 for the City of London, now in the National Galleries of Scotland (NG 2661).

Henry Pelham, Copley's half-brother, sits at a polished mahogany table with a flying squirrel tethered by a gold chain, a glass of water beside him. Shipped to London for the 1766 Society of Artists exhibition, the picture earned Copley election to the Society and Joshua Reynolds's qualified praise.

Thomas Mifflin, the Pennsylvania merchant and future first governor of the state, sits beside his wife Sarah Morris, who works at a small loom of fringed silk. Copley painted the double portrait in 1773, just before sailing for Europe, as a tribute to the non-importation movement that the Mifflins championed. The Philadelphia Museum of Art holds it.

The Boston merchant and town clerk Ezekiel Goldthwait sits in a wing chair with a ledger on the table beside him, his hand resting on the open page. Oil on canvas of 1771, paired with Copley's portrait of his wife Elizabeth at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, accession 41.85.

Hugh Montgomerie, future 12th Earl of Eglinton, stands in the scarlet uniform of the 77th Regiment of Foot against a wooded landscape suggesting the American frontier. Copley painted the full-length portrait in London in 1780 after Montgomerie's service in the French and Indian War, now held by the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

The Massachusetts merchant and slaveholder Isaac Royall sits in a damask-upholstered armchair in a green coat, the gilt frame and column behind him signalling rank. Now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the canvas belongs to Copley's Cambridge sittings of the late 1760s, before he left for Europe in 1774.

The teenage daughters of the Medford merchant Isaac Royall Jr. sit together with a small spaniel and a hummingbird tethered to a string. Painted around 1758 when Copley was twenty, the canvas is believed to be his first double portrait; the Loyalist Royalls fled to England in 1776, leaving it behind, and the Museum of Fine Arts acquired it in 1925.

Mary Toppan, newly married to the Salem merchant Benjamin Pickman, sits in a satin gown with a string of pearls at her throat, painted in 1763 when she was nineteen. The canvas is at the Yale University Art Gallery, accession 1966.79.3, and is one of Copley's earliest essays in the polished colonial manner he would carry to London.

Mary Turner Sargent leans on a pedestal beside a fountain, water cupped in her hand, in a Boston society portrait of 1763. The conceit of the basin and the pose derive from English mezzotints after Reynolds, sources Copley studied avidly in colonial Massachusetts before his move to London.

Elizabeth Oliver Watson, wife of the Boston merchant George Watson, sits in a russet silk gown holding a sprig of flowers. The 1765 portrait pairs with Copley's likeness of her husband and entered the Smithsonian American Art Museum as a gift from the family.

Mrs Humphrey Devereux, the artist's mother-in-law, sits in a satin gown with a lace cap, her hand resting on the carved arm of a chair. Copley painted the half-length portrait in oil on canvas in 1771 and shipped it from Boston to her in Halifax. It now hangs at the Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tamaki.

A young woman in a blue silk gown poses with one hand at her bodice, the other holding a length of pearls. Copley painted the half-length portrait in oil on canvas in 1771, near the end of his Boston decade in which he documented the merchant class of pre-Revolutionary New England.

Bust-length study of a Black sitter, possibly a London dockworker, made by Copley in 1777-78 as he prepared Watson and the Shark. The Detroit Institute of Arts holds the canvas, oil at 41.3 by 53.3 cm, which presents its subject as an individual at a moment when such treatment was rare in British painting.

Group portrait of the artist with his wife Susanna, their four children, and his Loyalist father-in-law Richard Clarke, painted in London after Copley fled the Revolution in 1775. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1777, the canvas announced Copley's arrival in British society and is now at the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

A naked Brook Watson founders in Havana harbour as a boat of rescuers strains toward him, with Morro Castle visible on the right and a Black sailor at the apex of the rescuing group. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1778 and now at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, the canvas dramatises an attack Watson survived as a fourteen-year-old cabin boy in 1749.

A girl in a blue silk dress holds a length of ribbon tied to a small bird while a spaniel rests at her side. Painted in Boston before Copley's departure for Europe, the portrait entered the Toledo Museum of Art and shows his close-observed treatment of fabric, fur, and feather.
collection-of-beauty-john-trumbull-gilbe: The history painter John Trumbull, in dark coat with white stock, faces the viewer in three-quarter profile. Stuart painted his fellow American while Trumbull was working in Washington on the four Revolutionary War scenes commissioned for the Capitol Rotunda; the canvas is at the Yale University Art Gallery.
collection-of-beauty-johnmontresorbycopl: Captain John Montresor, the British military engineer who surveyed Quebec and Detroit, sits in three-quarter view in his red officer's coat. Copley painted the portrait in oil on canvas around 1771, during his Boston practice before he left for London on the eve of the Revolution. The Detroit Institute of Arts holds the canvas.
collection-of-beauty-joseon-kang-huian-g: A Joseon scholar leans on a rocky outcrop, contemplating the flow of water below in the Daoist trope of the recluse-sage. Kang Hui-an, a fifteenth-century court official and painter, helped establish the Korean literati landscape idiom. The brushwork shows clear debts to early Ming academy masters in the Zhe school manner.
collection-of-beauty-joseph-brant-2: The Mohawk leader Thayendanegea, known to the British as Joseph Brant, appears bust-length in a fur-edged blue coat, silver gorget, and feathered headdress. Stuart painted Brant in London in 1785 during the Mohawk leader's diplomatic mission to negotiate land grants for Loyalist Iroquois resettled in Upper Canada after the American war.
collection-of-beauty-joseph-mallord-will: Embarking passengers and fishwives crowd the French pier as a squall builds beyond the harbour mouth. Turner had himself crossed to Calais in rough weather in 1802, and he exhibited this large canvas to challenge the marine paintings of his French contemporaries.

A vessel keels over on the East Anglian sands at low tide, attended by figures in the wet shallows. The work belongs to a group of Yarmouth sample studies Turner produced for engravers as test pieces in a more vaporous late manner. It is now part of the Turner Bequest at the National Gallery.

A rainbow arcs over Buttermere following a Lake District shower, the slate fells doubled in the still water below. Turner exhibited the picture at the Royal Academy aged twenty-three, after a Cumberland sketching tour. It is one of his earliest essays in the sublime mountain weather effects that would define him.

Local fisherwomen, the poissards, dig for lugworm bait on the broad expanse of Calais beach as the sun sinks behind them. Turner returned to the Channel coast repeatedly, treating Calais as the symbolic threshold between England and the Continent. The sky and wet sand dissolve into a single shimmering field of low light.

Harvesters work an open field on the Earl of Essex's estate at Cassiobury in Hertfordshire. The painting was a private commission produced alongside a series of watercolours of the park. It shows Turner extending his Claudean pastoral mode to a contemporary English country-house setting.

A loose oil sketch toward the large Trafalgar canvas commissioned by George IV for St James's Palace. Turner stitched together multiple moments of the engagement onto a single mast-cluttered composition. The freedom of brushwork here, intended only as a working study, anticipates his later, looser exhibited manner.

Boats tow a damaged sailing ship into the imaginary Dutch harbour of Port Ruysdael, Turner's homage to Jacob van Ruisdael. Painted late in his career, the canvas dissolves rigging and breaking sea into broad sweeps of grey, white and salt. It is one of several pictures in which Turner used invented Dutch place-names as a critical tribute.

Grenoble lies between the Drac and the distant snowfields of Mont Blanc, drawn during Turner's first Continental tour after the Peace of Amiens reopened France. The 1802 Alpine campaign permanently reshaped his sense of geological scale. The picture's stretched horizontal format prefigures his later panoramic mountain views.

A small, intimate study of a figure asleep, head sunk against bedding, kept in Turner's studio and bequeathed to the nation. The looseness of touch is closer to the colour-beginnings of his late watercolours than to anything he exhibited. It belongs to a private corpus of figurative sketches now in the Tate's Turner Bequest.

An Italian hill town rises above the misted Campagna, drawn from sketches Turner made on his second visit to Rome. The thinly washed watercolour leaves the paper itself standing in for the bleached southern light he prized.

A long horizontal sweep of Egremont's deer park with Tillington's spire pinning the horizon. One of the studies made in the Petworth studio Egremont set aside for him, the picture is structured almost entirely by golden, grazing light.

A view across the Earl of Egremont's lake, painted under the patronage that gave Turner the run of Petworth. Cool morning haze dissolves park, water and sky into the unified atmosphere typical of his Sussex landscapes.
An unpeopled stretch of cliff and surf treated as a study in elemental force. The thinly brushed sea and broken light show Turner's late shorthand for shoreline weather.

Merchant vessels ride the chop beside a stone breakwater in a dockside scene from Turner's early career, when he was building a reputation as a marine painter. The handling still leans on the Dutch seventeenth-century tradition of van de Velde.

Sails crowd the Solent off East Cowes, where Turner stayed with the architect John Nash during the 1827 Royal Yacht Club regatta. The picture belongs to a series of studies generated by that summer visit.

An oil sketch on canvas worked up while Turner was Nash's guest at East Cowes Castle. The yachts beating against the wind would be reorganised into the finished regatta picture exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1828.

A second oil sketch from the East Cowes regatta campaign, broadly laid in to test the disposition of the racing yachts. Turner used these large studies almost as colour rehearsals before committing to a finished exhibition picture.

Form is reduced to bands of gold, rose and slate water in a late, near-abstract evocation of dusk. Pictures of this kind, left in his studio at his death, anticipate by half a century the dissolutions of Impressionism.

An English river caught at the end of the day, with rushes and a low bank silhouetted against burning sky. The work belongs to the loose Thames oil sketches Turner made from his boat around Walton and Windsor.

Vessels lie at anchor under the red Devon cliffs of the Teign estuary, a coast Turner sketched repeatedly on his West Country tours. The watercolour links to his preparatory work for the Southern Coast engravings.

A close-quarters view of Nelson's flagship Victory at Trafalgar, taken from the mizen-shrouds rather than the more conventional broadside vantage. Turner had boarded Victory on her return to the Medway and used the sketches he made there to anchor the smoke-wreathed scene.

Estuary shipping gathers where Thames and Medway meet, painted in the tradition of seventeenth-century Dutch sea pieces. Heavy cloud and a low horizon underline Turner's command of English coastal weather.

Night falls on the battlefield as women search the heaped dead by torchlight, three years after the engagement. Turner had walked the ground himself; the picture quotes Byron's Childe Harold and refuses any patriotic triumph.

A poet implores his muse in a cramped attic, an unusually literary genre subject for Turner. Exhibited at the Royal Academy with verses of his own composition, it shows him courting the hierarchy of history painting.

A vertiginous Alpine gorge above the St Gotthard road, recorded on Turner's first Continental tour after the Peace of Amiens reopened Europe. The watercolour fed a series of Swiss subjects in which scale itself becomes the drama.

Storm and divine wrath sweep over a darkened Egyptian city as the firstborn die. An early bid for the prestige of Old Master history painting, the picture leans openly on Poussin's biblical compositions.

A quiet reach of the upper Thames painted from the boat Turner had fitted out as a floating studio. The fluid handling belongs to the Thames oil sketches in which he loosened his manner before the public ever saw it.

Most of the panel is given over to evening sky, with foliage massed at the lower edge and Guildford Castle barely indicated. The composition foreshadows Turner's later willingness to let weather dominate topography.

The Doge's Palace and the Riva degli Schiavoni shimmer through lagoon light in a late Venetian view. By his third trip to Venice in 1840 Turner was treating the city's stones as little more than coloured vapour.

The cliff-set Umbrian town floats above its golden plain in a picture begun and finished during Turner's second Roman stay. Exhibited at his studio on the Quattro Fontane, it greeted Italian visitors as a deliberate answer to Claude.
A pure marine, the canvas is given entirely to a churning sea raked by spray. Turner reportedly had himself lashed to a mast in storms; the picture's loose, scumbled paint claims that immediacy.
Cattle wade in the slow water below a country weir in one of Turner's pastoral Thames-valley sketches. The thin oil handling and silvery palette recall his admiration for Cuyp.

A screen of willows leans over still water in an unforced piece of Thames-side observation. It belongs to the group of Thames oil sketches on canvas that Turner kept in his studio rather than exhibiting; it entered the nation with the Turner Bequest in 1856.

The royal castle rides above the river on its chalk bluff, painted from Turner's boat on one of his summer Thames campaigns. Sky and water are set down in long, wet sweeps that leave the paint visibly mobile.

Fishermen drag a boat up onto a windswept beach beneath a heavy, scudding sky. Part of the Iveagh Bequest at Kenwood, the picture sits in Turner's lifelong dialogue with seventeenth-century Dutch marine painters such as van de Velde and Cuyp. Salt spray, wet sand and weather become as much the subject as the labour.

Agrippina steps ashore at Brundisium carrying the urn of her murdered husband Germanicus before a stage-set of imperial architecture. Conceived as the Ancient half of a paired Royal Academy exhibit, the canvas is built on Claudean perspective dissolved in Turner's own sun-soaked atmosphere.

The ruined Forum, then still grazed and known as the Campo Vaccino, glows under a luminous Roman evening. Painted as a pendant to Ancient Rome, it gave Turner one of his last great meditations on the city's layered time.

The Dutch admiral Maarten Tromp puts his ship about in heavy weather, a subject Turner returned to repeatedly in his last decade. The picture extends his admiration for the seventeenth-century Dutch marine tradition into a high-key, Romantic key.

The shattered piers of Caligula's pleasure-bridge at Baiae rise above a glassy bay in a moralised view of imperial vanity. Turner exhibited it at the Royal Academy with verses from his own Fallacies of Hope.

A tall-masted barge drifts past the island cemetery of San Michele in the Venetian lagoon. Painted alongside its Royal Academy companion the Dogano, the work converts a place of burial into a study of pearled morning light.

An early topographical watercolour from Turner's Cambridge tour, viewing Clare Hall and the soaring Perpendicular pinnacles of King's College Chapel across the Cam. Drawn at eighteen, the sheet shows the precise architectural draftsmanship that earned him admission to the Royal Academy schools.

A Thames-side prospect of the wooded Cliveden cliffs in Buckinghamshire, the river curling beneath in pale silver. Turner repeatedly returned to the Thames as a quintessentially English subject, here softening topography into atmospheric haze.

An apocalyptic sketch from the Book of Revelation, the spectral rider looming from a vortex of dark pigment. Painted around the time of his wife's death, the canvas pushes Turner's late, near-abstract handling of paint and his fascination with sublime terror.

A glassy Dutch harbour bathed in golden morning light, paying open homage to Aelbert Cuyp, whose paintings Turner studied on his 1817 Low Countries tour. The becalmed packet boat anchors a luminous sky that occupies more than half the canvas.

Westminster's old Palace blazes against the night sky on 16 October 1834, watched by a crowd massed on the Thames. Turner sketched the fire from a hired boat and produced two oil versions, of which this is the Philadelphia canvas. The conflagration let him paint exactly the kind of incandescent yellow-and-red sky he had been pursuing for decades.

The thundering Rheinfall in Switzerland, its spray rising into a churning sky encountered on Turner's first Continental tour after the Peace of Amiens. The painting marks his early engagement with the Alpine sublime that would shape his Romantic vocabulary.

A modest coastal cottage on the Kentish cliffs, rendered in the picturesque idiom Turner absorbed from Thomas Girtin and the watercolour tradition. The sheet dates from his teenage years working up topographical views for the print market.

Turner's first oil exhibited at the Royal Academy, depicting a fishing boat tossed beneath a cold moon off the Needles, Isle of Wight. The contrast of silver lunar light and orange lantern glow announces a lifelong preoccupation with luminous opposition.

Estuarine fishermen at low water on the Thames, the horizon line dropped to expose a vast, muted sky. The subdued grey-and-cream palette reflects Turner's study of seventeenth-century Dutch marine painters such as van de Velde.

Tyneside coal-heavers loading colliers under a full moon at Shields, painted as a pendant to a Venetian scene to contrast industrial north and southern lagoon. The torchlit smoke and silvered water typify Turner's late nocturnes.

The ruined Stewart royal palace above its loch in West Lothian, drawn from Turner's Scottish sketching tours undertaken for engraved topographical series. Soft watercolour washes blend the masonry into the surrounding landscape.

A panoramic survey of the capital seen from the hill at Greenwich, with the Queen's House and Wren's Royal Hospital below and St Paul's hazed in coal-smoke distance. The painting belongs to a series celebrating the Thames as the artery of empire.

The Augustinian ruin on the Wey in Surrey, its broken walls reflected in still water. Turner mined such Gothic remains for the picturesque subjects favoured by Romantic patrons and the engraving trade.

The Northumbrian border keep dissolving into rose and gold mist above the Tweed, a motif Turner painted repeatedly across his career. The late oil reduces architecture and cattle to translucent veils of pigment, anticipating modern abstraction.

A house portrait commissioned by the third Earl of Darlington, set in his County Durham deer park with a hunt in the foreground. Turner devotes the upper canvas to a churning, dramatic sky, signalling his shift from topography to Romantic landscape.

Naval shipping anchored at the Nore sandbank off the Kent dockyard, with rigging and bunting catching wet wind. Turner exhibited the canvas at his own gallery, courting comparison with Dutch marine masters in scale and atmosphere.

Working vessels labouring in the Thames estuary chop, sails braced against a low, weather-laden sky. The painting belongs to Turner's productive run of estuary subjects answering his rivalry with the marine tradition of van de Velde.

A paddle-steamer engulfed by a vortex of snow, smoke and sea, exhibited with Turner's claim that he had been lashed to the mast to observe it. Critics dismissed the canvas as 'soapsuds and whitewash', but it remains his definitive statement on the elemental sublime.

A solitary angler beside a wooded stream, painted in Turner's youthful picturesque manner. The watercolour reflects his early apprenticeship copying after Richard Wilson and the British landscape engravers.

An eyewitness response to the conflagration that destroyed the medieval Palace of Westminster, watched by crowds along the Thames. Turner sketched the blaze from a hired boat and translated it into pyrotechnic yellows and reds against the cool Westminster Bridge.

Sussex fisherfolk hauling their catch onto the shingle, with luggers and chalk cliffs receding behind. Turner repeatedly painted Hastings during the Napoleonic years when its beach was both a working port and a fashionable resort.

A bustling Norman harbour bathed in unnaturally Italianate light, criticised at the Royal Academy for its sun-drenched palette. The painting forms part of Turner's continental port series following his post-war travels to France.

Survivors clinging to lifeboats amid mountainous green seas, the doomed vessel rolling beyond. Engraved by Charles Turner, this was the first of the artist's canvases reproduced as a mezzotint, spreading his fame as a painter of catastrophe.

A lateen-sailed fishing boat departing the lagoon at dawn, its painted sail catching pink Adriatic light. Drawn from Turner's third Venetian visit, the canvas was accompanied by lines from his unfinished poem warning of storms ahead.

A reconstructed view of the Doric temple on Aegina, imagined intact above the Aegean, painted from sketches supplied by an architect-traveller as Turner himself never visited Greece. The canvas answered the British vogue for Hellenic antiquity stoked by the Elgin Marbles.

Nelson's flagship shown in three rotated views entering Sheerness with the admiral's body aboard, after Turner sketched her at anchor. The triple study reflects his marine fascination and the national mourning that followed Trafalgar.

A Highland packhorse bridge over the Tummel, recorded on Turner's 1801 Scottish tour that supplied subjects for engraved series and Walter Scott illustrations. The watercolour balances rugged geology against an open, weather-shifting sky.

A fantastical pairing of the water-nymph Undine, drawn from de la Motte Fouqué's novella, with the Neapolitan fisherman-rebel Masaniello. Painted at seventy-one, the canvas dissolves narrative into a swirl of aquatic colour typical of Turner's late square-format mythologies.
collection-of-beauty-joseph-wright-an-ir: A nocturnal interior of a Midlands forge, the white-hot bloom illuminating the ironworker's family. Wright was the painter of the early Industrial Revolution, treating bellows and tilt-hammers with the same chiaroscuro reverence Caravaggio gave to saints.
collection-of-beauty-joseph-wright-of-de: A Tyrrhenian lighthouse silhouetted against a cool, full moon over the Italian coast, recalled from Wright's 1773-75 sojourn near Naples. The painting exemplifies his fascination with competing light sources, here moonlight alone setting the spectral palette.

A silvered view of the Derbyshire valley of Dovedale under a full moon, its limestone crags and quiet river rendered in a cool, near-monochrome palette. Wright pursued nocturnes throughout his career, applying the dramatic chiaroscuro he developed for candlelit interiors to the open landscape.

An aged alchemist kneels before a glowing flask as phosphorus ignites in his laboratory, alluding to Hennig Brand's 1669 discovery. Wright stages the scene with the theatrical single-source illumination that defined his Enlightenment subjects, balancing scientific wonder against gothic shadow.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-1915-natu: A guitar, wine bottle, fruit dish and Bass ale with its red diamond logo sit on a checked tablecloth, the arrangement also legible as the head of a bull. Gris painted the 116-centimetre canvas in Paris in March 1915, shortly after returning from a wartime stay in the South of France; it entered the Metropolitan Museum of Art with the Leonard A. Lauder Cubist Collection in 2014.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-glass-and: A drinking glass and a folded checkerboard arranged on a tabletop in tightly interlocking planes of grey, black, and ochre. Painted around 1917 and held at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the panel belongs to Gris's late Synthetic Cubist phase, when he tightened the vocabulary toward crystalline geometry.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-jose-vict: A table holding a Médoc bottle, fruit dish, glass and a copy of Le Journal stands before a window looking onto a Montmartre balustrade and the trees of Place Ravignan. Gris painted the 115-centimetre canvas in 1915 from his studio in the Bateau-Lavoir; it is held by the Philadelphia Museum of Art and counts among his Synthetic Cubist breakthroughs.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-portrait-: A Cubist portrait of Picasso seated with a palette, his face and jacket broken into pale blue and ochre facets. Painted in 1912 and now at the Art Institute of Chicago, Gris inscribed the canvas 'Hommage à Pablo Picasso', framing his own analytic style as both tribute and challenge to the older master.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-still-lif: A mandolin, fruit dish, and folded newspaper arranged on a patterned tablecloth in flat, interlocking planes of muted blue, ochre, and white. Painted in 1919, the canvas belongs to Gris's Synthetic Cubist maturity, when he composed by deduction from geometric scaffolds before adding the objects rather than fragmenting them in.
collection-of-beauty-juan-legua-1911-jua: A seated man in dark suit and stiff collar tilts back in his chair, face splintered into a small grid of facets while the body remains legible. Painted in 1911 at 55 by 46 cm, the canvas is one of Gris's earliest Cubist portraits, the sitter a Spanish journalist living in Paris who likely used Juan Legua as a pen name. It is at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-judge-martin-howard: Judge Martin Howard sits in a brown coat with a sheaf of legal papers at his hand, painted in oil on canvas at 125.7 by 101 cm. The 1767 portrait is held by the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid, an unusual European home for a Copley colonial likeness.
collection-of-beauty-judische-hochzeit-i: Guests crowd a sunlit Tangier courtyard around dancers and musicians at a Sephardi wedding feast. Drawing on sketches from his 1832 North African journey with the Comte de Mornay, Delacroix translated direct observation into a Romantic ethnography rich in textile color and architectural detail.
collection-of-beauty-judit-decapitando-a: The biblical heroine and her maidservant pin the Assyrian general to his bed, blade drawn across his throat as blood spurts onto the linen. Gentileschi heightens the Caravaggesque tenebrism with a tightly compressed composition and the unflinching, muscular cooperation of the two women.
collection-of-beauty-judith-and-her-maid: In the aftermath of the killing, Judith pauses with sword raised while Abra wraps the severed head in a sack. A late Naples-period work, it returns to Gentileschi's signature subject in a quieter, more nocturnal register, lit by a single candle that gilds the drapery.
collection-of-beauty-jupiter-and-antiope: The Haarlem master, better known as a virtuoso engraver, treats the mythological seduction with a sculptural nude and the warm flesh tones he absorbed from his late Italian journey. Jupiter approaches in satyr disguise, the composition borrowed from Northern Mannerist prints Goltzius himself had popularised across Europe.
collection-of-beauty-jupiter-and-juno-an: A section of Annibale Carracci's fresco decoration of the Farnese Gallery in Rome, painted for Cardinal Odoardo Farnese and completed around 1602. The panel shows Juno, half-draped, coming to Jupiter on his couch, his eagle gripping a thunderbolt at the bedside and her peacock looking on; the scene is framed like an easel picture within an illusionistic surround of nude youths and feigned stone atlantes. The cycle of the Loves of the Gods made the gallery one of the founding monuments of Baroque ceiling painting.
collection-of-beauty-kagesue-takatsuna-a: Two mounted samurai surge through the rapids of the Uji in their famed race to lead the charge during the Genpei War. Kuniyoshi packs the triptych with churning water and twisting horses, exemplifying the warrior-print genre (musha-e) he revived in the late Edo period.
collection-of-beauty-kaigetsudo-ando-sta: A Yoshiwara courtesan stands alone in a richly patterned kimono, hip cocked in the languid S-curve that became the workshop's hallmark. As founder of the Kaigetsudō school, Ando concentrated entirely on monumental beauties, painted in fluid ink with broad swathes of color and gold on paper.
collection-of-beauty-kajikazawa-in-kai-p: A lone fisherman casts his net from a jagged outcrop while Mount Fuji rises pale beyond the surf. From the Thirty-six Views, the design is among Hokusai's most pared-down, reducing landscape to interlocking triangles printed in the imported Prussian blue (bero-ai) that defines the series.
collection-of-beauty-kalisz-rubens: Christ's body is lowered from the cross in a diagonal cascade of pale flesh and white shroud, supported by mourning saints. Rubens returned to this Counter-Reformation subject repeatedly after his Antwerp Cathedral altarpiece, modelling the dead Christ on classical sculpture studied during his years in Rome.
collection-of-beauty-kanae-yamamoto-1915: A cow rendered in sōsaku-hanga style, its bulk built up from carved planes of color. Yamamoto launched Japan's creative-print movement, insisting that the artist personally design, carve, and print the block, and his rural subjects helped redirect woodblock practice from commercial ukiyo-e toward modernist self-expression.
collection-of-beauty-kanae-yamamoto-1926: A view at the foot of Mount Tokkō in oils, painted after Yamamoto's return from Europe where he absorbed Post-Impressionist palette and brushwork. Better remembered for woodblock prints, he pursued painting alongside his advocacy for the children's free-drawing and farmers' art movements in interwar Japan.
collection-of-beauty-kanae-yamamoto-1938: An oil painting of Mount Fuji seen from Kami-Ide, a village at the foot of the mountain, painted by Yamamoto Kanae in 1938. The snow-streaked cone rises under drifting clouds beyond a foreground of plowed fields and autumn-red trees. Yamamoto, a pioneer of the sosaku-hanga creative print movement, devoted much of his later career to oil painting; the work is held by the Kanae Yamamoto museum in Ueda, Nagano.
collection-of-beauty-kanae-yamamoto-dutc: A color woodcut by Yamamoto Kanae of a girl in Dutch folk dress standing on a sandy path before a flat river landscape of fields, trees and a distant cottage, the scene built from broad, simplified planes of green and ochre. Yamamoto, the founding figure of Japan's sosaku-hanga movement of self-carved, self-printed artist's prints, took up European subjects of this kind in connection with his years of study in Europe from 1912 to 1916. The print is in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-kannon-riding-a-dra: The Buddhist bodhisattva of compassion rides a coiling dragon through cloudbanks, the figure modelled with the volumetric solidity of European academic painting. A Munich-trained pioneer of yōga (Western-style oil painting), Harada provoked debate by giving a Japanese religious subject the visual language of Counter-Reformation altarpieces.
collection-of-beauty-kano-eitoku-rakuchu: A panoramic bird's-eye survey of Kyoto in and around the capital, with thousands of tiny figures threading temples, markets and noble compounds amid gilded clouds. Eitoku codified the rakuchū rakugai zu format for the Momoyama elite; this pair was reportedly given by Oda Nobunaga to Uesugi Kenshin.
collection-of-beauty-kano-hideyori-maple: Courtiers picnic beneath flame-coloured maples on the slopes of Mount Takao, eating, dancing and flirting in vignettes spread across the gold-ground screen. One of the earliest surviving Japanese genre paintings, it shifts the Kano workshop's brush from Chinese-derived ink subjects toward the everyday life of contemporary Kyoto.
collection-of-beauty-kano-sansetsu-froli: Songbirds dart through the gnarled, almost calligraphic branches of a flowering plum and a weeping willow on a gold ground. Sansetsu, the eccentric heir of the Kyoto Kanō line, stylises nature into rhythmic arabesques, pushing the school's bird-and-flower repertoire toward a mannered late-Momoyama elegance.
collection-of-beauty-karl-brullov-the-la: Citizens of Pompeii stumble through the streets as columns crack, lightning splits the sky and ash falls across the doomed city under Vesuvius. Painted in 1830-33 in Rome on commission from Count Anatoly Demidov, the vast canvas, 4.6 by 6.5 metres, won the gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1834 and now belongs to the State Russian Museum.
collection-of-beauty-karl-bryullov-bryul: Bathsheba at her bath, attended by a black servant beside a fountain in a walled garden. Bryullov worked on the large canvas for three years without finishing it, and the painting now hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow, the surface marked by a tear traditionally attributed to a boot the frustrated artist hurled at it.
collection-of-beauty-karl-friedrich-abel: The composer Carl Friedrich Abel sits with his viola da gamba and a sheet of manuscript, a virtuoso of the instrument and Gainsborough's close friend. Abel and Johann Christian Bach ran the Bach-Abel concert series in London from 1765, and the painter, himself an amateur gambist, owned several Abel autograph scores.
collection-of-beauty-karl-friedrich-schi: An allegorical tribute to the Prussian industrial reformer Peter Beuth, shown astride Pegasus as he soars over a panorama of human civilisation and progress. The composition fuses Romantic landscape with Enlightenment allegory, celebrating Beuth's role in the modernisation of the Prussian state.

An imagined Greek polis spreads along a rocky promontory, temples and stoa stacked up the slope toward a fortified acropolis. Schinkel painted the canvas in Berlin around 1806, years before his architectural career began, channelling his early training as a stage and panorama painter into archaeological reverie.

Dawn light spreads across a placid river valley as a small boat puts out from the shore. Although the file references Schinkel, the work belongs to the meditative landscape mode of early-nineteenth-century German Romanticism, where the simple act of daybreak carries the weight of spiritual allegory.

The Queen of the Night appears on a crescent moon beneath a vast hemispherical vault of stars, in Karl Friedrich Schinkel's set design for Mozart's Die Zauberflote. The gouache on paper, about 46 by 61 centimetres, was made around 1815 for the production staged at the Berlin Royal Opera in 1816 and is held in the Kupferstichkabinett of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin. The starry hall became the most reproduced of Schinkel's stage designs and one of the most famous opera sets of the nineteenth century.

A spired Gothic cathedral rises atop a cliff above the sea, more vision than topography. The motif - architecture as sacred outcropping - belongs to the shared Romantic imagination of Schinkel and Friedrich, where the medieval church stands in for a yearned-for unity of faith, nation and landscape.

A vast Gothic cathedral towers over a riverside town at sunset, its silhouette dwarfing the mortal traffic on the quay. The motif of the imagined medieval Dom appealed to Romantic painters as both architectural dream and patriotic emblem after the Napoleonic Wars.

A fortified castle commands the bend of a broad river under a luminous, theatrical sky. The composition treats architecture scenographically, the way Schinkel did in his stage designs for Berlin, while the contemplative figures and burnished light belong to the wider Romantic landscape current.

A natural rock arch frames a distant view, conceived as the Nordic pendant to a sunlit Italian landscape. The pairing stages a Romantic dialogue between the sublime German wilderness and the classical south, a polarity that runs through the era's painting and through Schinkel's own architectural imagination.
collection-of-beauty-karl-joseph-stieler: The young daughter of a Greek War of Independence hero is shown in embroidered Greek costume, her dark hair loose beneath a tasselled cap. Stieler painted the portrait for Ludwig I of Bavaria's Schönheitengalerie, the Munich gallery of beauties in which the king collected idealised female likenesses.
collection-of-beauty-karolina-lizius: The shoemaker's daughter Karolina Lizius gazes outward in modest dress, painted as one of the bourgeois sitters Ludwig I added to his Schönheitengalerie. Stieler, court painter in Munich, specialised in this restrained Biedermeier portrait formula: smooth finish, neutral ground, demure psychology.
collection-of-beauty-katsushika-hokusai-: Pilgrims bathe in the falls at Ōyama, where Rōben is said to have purified himself before founding the mountain's temple. From A Tour of the Waterfalls of the Provinces, Hokusai abstracts cascading water into ribbons of stylised line, treating each fall as a graphic emblem of place.

Yoshitsune's retainers wash their horses beneath the Yoshino falls, the cascade splitting into braided ribbons of pale paper. The plate from the Waterfalls series fuses warrior legend with landscape, characteristic of how Hokusai layered narrative into his late topographical print sets.

The Kirifuri ("falling mist") cascade on Mount Kurokami breaks into four white tendrils against dark cliffs, with tiny travellers gazing up from below. Hokusai's Waterfalls series treats Japan's sacred falls as near-abstract patterns, the water carved as flat decorative line rather than naturalistic spray.

Travellers and packhorses pause on the Kisokaidō highway beside the Ono falls, dwarfed by a smooth blue sheet of water. From the Tour of the Waterfalls, the print pairs Hokusai's stylised, almost geometric treatment of cascades with the everyday traffic of one of Edo Japan's great post roads.

From the celebrated series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, this woodblock print depicts the towering Amida Falls cascading from a circular pool said to resemble the head of the Buddha Amida. Hokusai pairs sweeping calligraphic line with flat planes of indigo and ochre, dwarfing tiny travellers beside the rushing water.

Cherry-blossom viewers gather on the bluff at Goten-yama overlooking Edo Bay, with Mount Fuji a faint cone on the horizon. Part of the Thirty-six Views, the print binds a popular hanami spot to the sacred mountain through Hokusai's careful balancing of human ritual and distant geology.

A canary alights on a bowed peony stem against a deep blue sky, accompanied by a haiku. From Hokusai's Large Flowers series for the publisher Eijudō, the print compresses the kachō-e bird-and-flower tradition into a tight diagonal, exploiting the new Prussian blue pigment for luminous backgrounds.

A polychrome woodblock print from Hokusai's series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, published around 1830-32, known as Rainstorm Beneath the Summit (Sanka haku-u). While the peak of Fuji stands clear against drifting clouds, a storm breaks over the lower slopes and a jagged bolt of red lightning flashes across the darkened base of the mountain. The design is the stormy counterpart to the serene Fine Wind, Clear Morning, and ranks with the Great Wave among the most celebrated images of the series.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-ebisu-11: A quiet harbour scene from the Souvenirs of Travel II series, capturing a wooden boat at the small port of Ebisu on Sado Island. Kawase, a leading shin-hanga artist, renders the wet stone and overcast sky in muted, atmospheric washes that revive the woodblock tradition for the modern era.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-hasui-1931-s: Thick snow falls through a darkening sky onto a boat landing at Mukojima, on the bank of Tokyo's Sumida River: moored boats lie blanketed in white, a stilt-built boathouse glows from within, and a lone ferryman crosses the still water. The 1931 color woodblock print shows Hasui's shin-hanga manner at its most atmospheric, using graded blues and untouched white paper to carry the weight of the snowfall. Snow scenes such as this became the works for which he is best remembered.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-hasui-no-ser: Kawase Hasui's final print design, published in 1957, the year of his death. Snow-covered stone steps climb between snow-laden cedars toward the hall sheltering the Konjikido, the famed Golden Hall of Chuson-ji temple at Hiraizumi, while a lone figure ascends under an umbrella through the falling snow. The design is traditionally honored as the artist's zeppitsu, or last work.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-tenno-ji-27: Plate from the Souvenirs of Travel III series, depicting the precincts of the ancient Shitennō-ji temple in Osaka. Kawase's shin-hanga method preserves Edo-period block-cutting techniques while indulging Western sensibilities for soft light and weather, here a damp, lantern-lit dusk.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-zojoji: View of the Tokugawa mortuary temple Zōjō-ji at Shiba, from the Twenty Views of Tokyo series. A solitary figure shelters under a paper umbrella as snow falls against the vermilion gate, a hallmark of Kawase's quiet, weather-soaked urban landscapes.
collection-of-beauty-kazimir-malevich-su: Coloured rectangles and bars float on a white field, freed from any object reference. Malevich exhibited his first Suprematist canvases at the Last Futurist Exhibition 0,10 in Petrograd on 19 December 1915, declaring painting's right to non-objective form; he hung the Black Square in the corner traditionally reserved for the household icon.
collection-of-beauty-keisai-eisen-wasser: A coiling water dragon, or mizuchi, from a late ukiyo-e series devoted to birds, beasts, insects and fish. Eisen, better known for bijin-ga prints of Edo women, here adapts the colour woodblock to a more decorative, naturalist mode in keeping with kacho-e tradition.
collection-of-beauty-kenko-shokei-shosho: Ink-painting from the Zen monk-painter's interpretation of the Eight Views of Xiao and Xiang, the canonical Chinese landscape suite of distant temples, mist and migrating geese. Shōkei trained in Kamakura under Geiami and brought a flecked, slightly nervous brush to the Muromachi suiboku tradition.
collection-of-beauty-khnopff-listening-t: A figure buries her face in her hand as a half-glimpsed pianist plays in the corner, the music itself unseen. Khnopff, a founding Belgian Symbolist, isolates inwardness and silence with his characteristic muted palette and severe, almost photographic restraint.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-chuseon: An autumn night landscape illustrating Ouyang Xiu's prose poem on the sound of autumn, the Chuseongbu, with wind-bent trees, distant mountains, and the Song poet's calligraphy occupying the upper half of the silk. Kim Hongdo painted it in 1805, late in his career as Joseon Korea's leading court painter, fusing Chinese literary subject with his characteristic ink-wash atmosphere.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-feast-f: Officials and attendants gather around low banquet tables inside the Pyongyang governor's hall, with dancers and musicians arranged on the floor below. The painting is the first scroll in Kim Hong-do's three-part series documenting an official feast, executed in the documentary genre painting style of late Joseon court commissions.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-hwaseon: A scene from the Eight Views of Hwaseong attributed to Kim Hong-do, the fortress wall snaking along a ridge toward a hilltop command pavilion above the new royal city of Suwon. As court painter to King Jeongjo, Kim documented the fortress completed in 1796 in the ink-and-light-colour idiom of late Joseon topographic painting.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-kyujang: Painted view of Kyujanggak, the royal library founded in 1776 on the grounds of Changdeokgung by King Jeongjo. Kim Hong-do, the king's designated painter, produced this colour-on-paper record at the moment the institution was established, documenting one of Jeongjo's major cultural undertakings.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-samgong: A long horizontal handscroll in ink and colour on silk, Samgongbulhwando contrasts the freedom of nature with the burdens of office through scenes of recluses and scholars in mountain retreats. Kim Hong-do painted the scroll in 1801, measuring 133.7 by 418.4 cm and now held by the Leeum Samsung Museum of Art in Seoul.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-songhac: A drunken Buddhist monk lies sprawled beneath a gnarled pine, a wine cup tipped beside him as a young attendant looks on. Kim Hong-do, the leading court painter of the late Joseon era, worked the subject in ink and light colour on paper around 1800, mixing genre humour with the literati ideal of the inebriated sage.
collection-of-beauty-king-lear-and-corde: The mad Lear, crowned in wildflowers, is reunited with the kneeling Cordelia at the French camp in Act IV, scene 7 of Shakespeare's tragedy. West painted the canvas in 1793 for John Boydell's Shakespeare Gallery; it now belongs to the Folger Shakespeare Library.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-1913-stree: Two cocottes in feathered hats and fur stoles stride down a Berlin pavement, a crowd of dark-suited men pressing past on either side. Oil on canvas, 120.6 x 91 cm, the picture belongs to Kirchner's Berlin Strassenbilder cycle of 1913-15 and is held by the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-farbentanz: Two pairs of figures lock arms in a flat dance, the bodies rendered in unmodelled planes of red, blue, green and yellow. The composition belongs to Kirchner's late Davos period, when, working in the Swiss Alps after his breakdown, he flattened his Brücke expressionism into broad colour fields influenced by his contact with Picasso's neoclassical work.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-sand-hills: Pale dunes outside the Berlin suburb of Grünau roll in jagged ridges under a sharp blue sky, with a few small figures scattered across the slope. Kirchner painted the picture in 1913 during a summer excursion from his new Berlin studio; the canvas was photographed for the Google Art Project from a German museum collection.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-self-portr: Kirchner stands in his studio in army uniform with the bloodied stump of an amputated right hand, a nude model behind him in sickly yellow tones. The 1915 oil at the Allen Memorial Art Museum, Oberlin, references his service in the 75th Field Artillery Regiment and the breakdown that brought a provisional discharge; it was later included in the Nazi Entartete Kunst exhibition of 1937.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-zwei-fraue: Erna and Gerda Schilling stand by a washbasin in a Berlin interior, one bending forward to dip her hands while the other looms behind in pointed silhouette. Kirchner painted the dancer sisters repeatedly during his Berlin period; the canvas is in the Städel Museum, Frankfurt, with sharp pink and green complementaries pitched against the city's nervous tempo.
collection-of-beauty-kisokaido14-itahana: The fourteenth station on the inland Kisokaidō highway, from the celebrated series Eisen and Hiroshige produced jointly in the 1830s. Eisen contributes a snowbound village under a heavy grey sky, peasants leaning into the wind in the bokashi-graded foreground.
collection-of-beauty-kitagawa-utamaro-ha: From the Twelve Types of Women's Handicraft series, an elegant ukiyo-e study of a kamiyui dressing a client's elaborate coiffure. Utamaro's signature bijinga close-up, pale ground and supple linework foreground the intimate gestures of female labour in the pleasure quarters.
collection-of-beauty-kitagawa-utamaro-ta: Ohisa, a celebrated Edo teahouse beauty, inspects the back of her coiffure with paired mirrors during the Asakusa autumn festival. Utamaro's precise hairlines and luminous mica-dusted ground typify his bust-portrait okubi-e of fashionable contemporary women.
collection-of-beauty-kiyonaga-bathhouse-: Half of a celebrated diptych depicting women in a public bathhouse, an unusually informal subject from the Tenmei era. Kiyonaga, head of the Torii school, sets his tall, calm figures in the careful spatial recession that reformed bijinga for the next generation.
collection-of-beauty-kiyonobu-yamanaka-i: Two kabuki actors square off in a confrontational pose typical of aragoto bravura roles. Kiyonobu, founder of the Torii line of theatre artists, defined the early ukiyo-e print with bold contour lines and the hand-applied tan-e orange-red pigment characteristic of pre-polychrome woodblock work.
collection-of-beauty-konrad-witz-004: Saint Christopher wades through dark water bearing the Christ Child, his giant frame sharply lit against a wooded shore. Witz, working in Basel, was an early Northern realist whose granular textures and naturalistic landscape settings broke with International Gothic abstraction.
collection-of-beauty-korinsscreen: A pair of folding screens depicting the rocky pine-clad islets of Matsushima Bay, with stylised waves curling in gold-leaf and malachite green. Kōrin, leading master of the Rinpa school, treats the famed scenic site as flat decorative pattern rather than topographic record.
collection-of-beauty-kuniyoshi-utagawa-a: A waterside Edo scene along the Sumida, the river that defined the city's ferry traffic, festivals and pleasure boating. Kuniyoshi, an Utagawa-school designer best known for warrior prints, here turns to a quieter genre subject in the bold linework typical of late ukiyo-e.
collection-of-beauty-kuniyoshi-utagawa-p: Devotees perform misogi, the Shinto cold-water purification rite, beneath a thundering cascade. Kuniyoshi exploits the vertical ōban format to dramatise the columnar fall of water, a theatrical staging that recalls his celebrated heroic and supernatural compositions.
collection-of-beauty-kuniyoshi-utagawa-t: A hanging scroll depicting the arhat Handaka Sonja, shaven-headed and large-eared, summoning a dragon from his begging bowl amid a coiling rain cloud. Kuniyoshi handles the Buddhist iconography in ink and pale colour with the muscular drawing he refined in his warrior prints.
collection-of-beauty-kuroda-seiki-kohan0: Lakeside, painted at Hakone, shows the artist's wife seated by the water in a yukata, a paper fan in her lap. Kuroda, who trained in Paris, brought plein-air Impressionist colour and the high-key palette of yōga oil painting back to Meiji Japan.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-goluboydo: The Blue House, a stout provincial dwelling with a corner shop and figures going about their day on the sun-warmed pavement. Boris Kustodiev returned obsessively to small Russian towns and merchant life, painting them in saturated colour from his Petersburg studio after illness confined him to a wheelchair from 1916.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-merchants: A young merchant's wife sits before a samovar laden with cakes, watermelon, and grapes, her cat resting on the table beside her. Painted in 1918 and held at the State Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg, the picture is one of Kustodiev's most reproduced canvases, an elegy for the pre-revolutionary provincial bourgeoisie composed from a bed where polio confined him.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-promenade: Townsfolk in summer hats and dresses stroll along the Volga embankment at Tutaev, the white-walled Romanov-Borisoglebsky churches rising behind them. Painted in 1909 in oil on canvas at 100 by 125 cm, the work marks Kustodiev's turn toward provincial merchant life as a subject. The picture is in the State Russian Museum.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-renee-not: Renée Ivanovna Notgaft sits in a contemplative half-length pose, her dress and bare shoulders set against a darker backdrop. Kustodiev painted the portrait in 1914, the year before his spinal illness confined him to a wheelchair and pushed him toward the bright, festive Russian subjects of his late work.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-russian-v: A bare-breasted bather stands in a wooden bathhouse, gripping a birch besom, with steam and a samovar behind her. Painted in 1925 to 26, the canvas was Kustodiev's last major work, completed from his wheelchair on the reverse of an older student composition because canvas was scarce; it now hangs in the Nizhny Novgorod State Art Museum.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-self-port: Kustodiev paints himself in fur cap and overcoat against a snowy Russian street, hand to chin in a moment of pause. Commissioned in 1912 for the Uffizi self-portrait gallery in Florence, the picture places the artist within the Russian merchant world he was making his subject.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-the-bolsh: A giant Bolshevik in winter coat and felt boots strides over the rooftops of Moscow carrying an enormous red banner, with crowds streaming through the streets below. Painted in 1920 and held at the Tretyakov Gallery, the canvas reads as both celebration and warning, its scale rhetoric drawn from icon and lubok traditions Kustodiev had absorbed in his pre-war work.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-trinity-d: Villagers in bright Sunday clothes gather under birches for the Orthodox feast of the Trinity, with onion-domed churches behind them. Painted in 1920, the canvas belongs to Kustodiev's cycle of provincial holiday scenes composed from memory during his confinement to a wheelchair, an idealised reconstruction of pre-revolutionary peasant ritual.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-voloshin: Portrait of the Symbolist poet and critic Maximilian Voloshin, painted in 1924. By that date Kustodiev had been confined to a wheelchair for eight years after spinal surgery, working almost entirely from photographs and sittings arranged at his Petrograd apartment.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiev-winter-sh: Sledges glide through a snowbound Russian provincial town during the carnival week before Lent, with onion-domed churches and crowds of fairgoers under a pink winter sky. Painted in 1919 at the height of the Civil War, Kustodiev's nostalgic merrymaking belongs to a cycle of Maslenitsa scenes that imagined the lost merchant culture as folk pageantry.
collection-of-beauty-kustodievb-provinc: A bustling provincial Russian street scene, with painted shop signs, market stalls, and townspeople in coloured kerchiefs and caftans. Kustodiev painted dozens of these idealized merchant-town pictures in the 1910s and 1920s, working from memory and old sketches after a spinal tumour left him paralysed below the waist.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiyev-fair: A provincial Russian fair in full swing, traders' awnings and lacquered toys crowding a wooden square under a summer sky. Painted in 1910 and held by the Nizhny Novgorod State Museum of Fine Arts, the canvas grew out of Kustodiev's Volga travels and his fascination with market days as folk theatre.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiyev-mate: The engraver Vasily Mathé (1856-1917) sits at his work table, the older man portrayed with the bookish concentration of a long career in printmaking. Painted by Kustodiev in 1902 while still close to his Repin training, the portrait honours the teacher who supervised the artist's etching studies at the Academy.
collection-of-beauty-kustodiyevsemenov-k: The young physicists Pyotr Kapitsa and Nikolai Semyonov sit shoulder to shoulder over a workbench, both still in their twenties. Painted by Kustodiev in 1921 after Kapitsa joked that they would one day win Nobel Prizes, the canvas was paid for with two pounds of flour and a cockerel, and remains with the Kapitsa family.
collection-of-beauty-l-embarquement-pour: Lovers prepare to leave the island of Venus in golden afternoon light, a melancholic departure rather than the arrival the title might suggest. Watteau's reception piece for the Académie royale invented the genre of the fête galante, with feathery brushwork drawn from his study of Rubens.
collection-of-beauty-l-enlevement-des-sa: Roman soldiers seize the Sabine women at Romulus's signal in a frieze of taut, sculptural figures arrayed before classical architecture. Poussin choreographs the violence with archaeological detail and disciplined gesture, exemplifying the rational French classicism he forged in Rome.
collection-of-beauty-l-enlevement-par-pa: An early figural composition treating the rape of Persephone by Pluto in dark, churning paint and a fevered ochre-and-black palette. Cézanne dedicated the canvas to his friend Émile Zola; it dates from the violent, romantic phase that preceded his Impressionist conversion at Pontoise.
collection-of-beauty-l-ermitage-par-paul: Cover lithograph for the Symbolist literary review L'Ermitage, depicting a pensive woman wreathed in stylised foliage. Berthon, a pupil of Eugène Grasset, worked in soft chalky tones rather than Mucha's saturated colour, giving his Art Nouveau posters a distinctive fresco-like flatness.
collection-of-beauty-l-homme-au-bonnet-d: A seated man in a white cotton cap, his face built up in thick ridges of paint. Oil on canvas, painted in 1866 and held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. The sitter is the artist's uncle Dominique Aubert, whom Cézanne painted in a series of portraits laid in heavily with the palette knife, a phase he later called couillarde.
collection-of-beauty-l-l-boilly-une-loge: Spectators crowd a theatre box on a free-admission performance day, a working-class audience pressed shoulder to shoulder. Boilly titled the panel 'Une loge, un jour de spectacle gratuit'; the small oil measures 32.5 by 41.7 cm and hangs in the Musée Lambinet at Versailles.
collection-of-beauty-l-ultimo-bacio-di-g: Romeo, foot already on the balcony, embraces Juliet in an exchange of literary tenderness laced with foreboding. Hayez, the leading Italian Romantic painter and a quiet Risorgimento sympathiser, modelled the composition on theatrical tableaux to charge it with patriotic feeling.
collection-of-beauty-la-batalla-de-casci: Florentine soldiers scramble naked from the Arno after a false Pisan alarm, twisting their bodies as they grab for arms on the bank. The composition survives only through Bastiano da Sangallo's 1542 grisaille copy at Holkham Hall, the lost cartoon Michelangelo prepared in 1504 for the Palazzo Vecchio having served as a school of anatomy for a generation of Florentine artists.
collection-of-beauty-la-bohemienne-endor: A lion sniffs at a sleeping Black musician beside a moonlit river, lute and water jar at her side. Rousseau's flattened forms, dreamlike disjunctions and meticulous storybook clarity show the self-taught douanier inventing a modern visionary mode admired by the Parisian avant-garde.
collection-of-beauty-la-continence-de-sc: The Roman general Scipio refuses the captive Iberian princess offered as spoils of war, gesturing for her return to her betrothed Allucius. Pittoni painted the moral exemplum in 1733, one of many Venetian treatments of the Livy episode in the pale, sweetened palette he favoured.
collection-of-beauty-la-debacle-monet-w5: The breakup of ice on the Seine after a hard winter near Vétheuil, with floes drifting past bare riverbanks. Monet returned to this motif repeatedly in 1880, using broken brushwork to register the shifting interplay of water, ice and reflected sky.
collection-of-beauty-la-famille-lafitte-: A group portrait of the Laffite family by the leading court painter of Louis XIV. Rigaud's studio specialised in elaborate full-length likenesses of French nobility, with rich drapery, polished flesh tones and carefully posed sitters that established the visual vocabulary of Bourbon state portraiture.
collection-of-beauty-la-foire-chinoise: Figures in fanciful Eastern dress mingle at a market under bamboo awnings, monkeys and exotic birds scattered through the stalls. Boucher designed the canvas around 1742 as part of his chinoiserie cycle for the Beauvais tapestry manufactory, where the cartoons supplied a long-running suite of woven panels.
collection-of-beauty-la-fornarina-by-raf: Long identified as the baker's daughter Margherita Luti, Raphael's lover, the sitter wears an oriental turban and a slim arm-band inscribed with the painter's name. The picture, completed near the end of Raphael's life, has the tactile sfumato modelling and direct erotic charge of his late Roman period.
collection-of-beauty-la-grande-piscine-d: An Orientalist interior depicting the great bath at Bursa in Ottoman Anatolia. Gérôme combined ethnographic observation from his eastern travels with academic precision, treating tilework, steam and bathers' bodies with the same hard-edged finish that made his Eastern scenes so widely reproduced.
collection-of-beauty-la-inmaculada-conce: The Virgin rises on a tide of cherubs against a stormy sky, hands joined in prayer above the moon and lily of the Immaculate iconography. Begun by El Greco in his last years and finished by his son Jorge Manuel after 1614, the canvas now hangs in the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.
collection-of-beauty-la-liberte-guidant-: An allegorical Liberty, bare-breasted and clutching the tricolore, leads insurgents over a barricade strewn with the dead during the July Revolution of 1830. Delacroix, the standard-bearer of French Romanticism, fuses contemporary reportage with classical personification in vivid, brushy oil.
collection-of-beauty-la-peche-chinoise: Anglers in pagoda hats cast their lines from a delicate wooden bridge while attendants prepare baskets on the bank. Boucher painted the piece around 1742 as another panel of the Beauvais chinoiserie cycle, his fantasy China assembled from imported porcelains and traveller's prints rather than direct observation.
collection-of-beauty-la-pisanella-by-l-b: Set design for the Port of Famagusta, the Cypriot harbour from Gabriele d'Annunzio's play La Pisanelle ou la Mort parfumée. Bakst made the watercolour in 1913 for Ida Rubinstein's production at the Théâtre du Châtelet, staged by Vsevolod Meyerhold with music by Ildebrando Pizzetti.
collection-of-beauty-la-ronda-de-noche-p: Captain Frans Banning Cocq in black with red sash steps forward giving the order to march, Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch in pale yellow strides beside him, and the company tumbles into motion behind. Signed and dated 1642, the canvas of 363 by 437 cm in the Rijksmuseum is the largest of the Amsterdam civic-guard group portraits.
collection-of-beauty-la-route-de-vetheui: A snow-effect view of the road leading into Vétheuil, the Seine-side village where Monet lived from 1878. The picture belongs to his series of winter landscapes painted en plein air, the broken brushwork registering the muted blues and lilacs of low northern light on settled snow.
collection-of-beauty-la-seine-a-lavacour: A sunlit stretch of the Seine opposite Vétheuil, painted in the years Monet spent there following his wife Camille's death. The exhibition-scale canvas, accepted at the 1880 Salon, shows him reconciling Impressionist broken touch with the broader, calmer compositions of mid-career.
collection-of-beauty-la-seine-a-vetheuil: The Seine at Vétheuil, the riverside village where Monet settled in 1878 after leaving Argenteuil. Soft poplars and reflections built up in short, drily loaded strokes typify the more sober palette of his late-1870s landscapes.
collection-of-beauty-la-table-de-cuisine: A kitchen table crowded with a fruit basket, pots and a folded cloth, the tabletop tipped sharply toward the viewer. Oil on canvas worked between 1888 and 1890, now in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris. Cézanne tilts the planes and crops the cloth at the lower edge to make geometric form, not accurate space, the subject.
collection-of-beauty-la-vision-apres-le-: Breton women in white coiffes lean forward in prayer, their vision of Jacob wrestling the angel materialising across a vermilion field divided by an apple tree. Painted at Pont-Aven in 1888 and now in the National Galleries of Scotland, the canvas is the breakthrough work in which Gauguin abandoned naturalistic colour for symbolic, cloisonné planes outlined in dark blue.
