The defeated Persian queen and her household kneel before Alexander the Great after Issus, in a vast frieze-like composition acquired by London's National Gallery in 1857. Veronese fills the picture with contemporary Venetian costume, courtly architecture, and a noble gesture of clemency.
collection-of-beauty-paris-art-deco-boil: The sculptor Jean-Antoine Houdon at work in his studio, modelling a clay bust of the astronomer Pierre-Simon Laplace. Oil on canvas, about 1803, in the Musée des Arts décoratifs, Paris. Finished casts and tools fill the cluttered workshop behind the seated sculptor.
collection-of-beauty-parmigianino-004: Parmigianino's celebrated late altarpiece, in which the serpentine Madonna cradles an unusually elongated Christ Child. The exaggerated proportions and ambiguous architecture exemplify the Mannerist taste for grace pushed beyond classical norm.
collection-of-beauty-parmigianino-madonn: Known as the Madonna of the Long Neck, this unfinished altarpiece is a touchstone of Italian Mannerism. Parmigianino elongates the Virgin's anatomy and tilts the spatial logic of the column and miniature prophet for an unsettling, refined elegance.
collection-of-beauty-parting-spring-by-k: The left panel of a pair of folding screens by Kawai Gyokudō, designated an Important Cultural Property of Japan. Working in the nihonga tradition, the artist evokes the melancholy of late spring through misty mountains and falling cherry blossoms.

The right panel of Gyokudō's Parting Spring screens, completing a continuous landscape of waterfalls, drifting petals, and veiled peaks. The nihonga master fuses traditional ink technique with subtle modern atmospheric effect.
collection-of-beauty-patenierchristopher: Saint Christopher wades across a wide river bearing the Christ Child on his shoulder, dwarfed by a panoramic landscape of jagged rocks, distant towns and luminous water. The sweeping high viewpoint is characteristic of Patinir, often credited as the first specialist in Western landscape painting.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-1892-9: Two Provençal labourers face off across a wine bottle in Cézanne's most distilled treatment of the card-players theme. The Courtauld version reduces the cast to its essential pair, the figures built from the planar, faceted strokes that prefigured Cubism.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-bather: A group of male nudes along a riverbank, some standing and some reclining, set into an open landscape. Oil on canvas of about 1890, part of the bather series Cézanne pursued from the 1870s onward, now in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris. The figures are built to structure the space rather than to display the flesh.

A group of nude bathers is arranged beneath arching trees that frame the composition like a vault, their bodies echoing the leaning trunks. One of three large Baigneuses Cézanne worked on between 1894 and 1905; this canvas is in the National Gallery, London. He sacrificed individual likeness to fit the figures to the triangular structure of the trees.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-boutei: A dark bottle, a glass carafe, a stoneware jug and a scatter of lemons stand on a draped table. Watercolour and graphite on paper of about 1902 to 1906, in the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid. Cézanne left much of the sheet bare, letting the white paper carry the highlights between thin washes.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-french: Nude female figures arranged in two groups beneath a vault of leaning trees, the bodies pared to broad blue and ochre planes. The largest of Cézanne's Bather canvases, oil on canvas, about 210 by 251 cm, worked on over roughly seven years and left unfinished at his death in 1906. It entered the Philadelphia Museum of Art in 1937.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-houses: Pale ochre houses clustered on a plateau above the Riaux valley, the rocky hillside built up in cool blues and greens beneath a high sky. Oil on canvas painted around 1883 near L'Estaque on the Mediterranean coast, now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington. Cézanne worked the terrain in faceted planes of colour rather than line.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-le-gra: An adolescent boy mid-stride in a pale watery landscape, hands on his hips, his body slightly out of proportion. Oil on canvas of about 1885 based on a studio photograph of a posed model, now in the Museum of Modern Art, New York, from the Lillie P. Bliss Collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-madame: Hortense Fiquet, the painter's wife, sits in three-quarter view wearing a broad green hat, her hands folded in her lap. Oil on canvas of about 1891 to 1892, catalogued BF141 in the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia. Cézanne built the face and bodice from planes of dull violet, ochre and grey-green laid side by side.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-maison: A small ochre farmhouse, the Maison Maria, sits among pines on the road to the Château Noir near Aix-en-Provence. Oil on canvas of about 1895, in the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth. Cézanne worked the ground and foliage in parallel diagonal strokes of green, blue and orange.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-montag: Cézanne returned obsessively to the limestone ridge near his native Aix-en-Provence, structuring its slopes through patches of constructive brushwork. The painting treats landscape as an architecture of colour planes, foundational for early modernism.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-pyrami: Four human skulls are stacked in a low pyramid on a bare tabletop against a dark ground. Oil on canvas painted between about 1898 and 1900, the only Cézanne to push the skulls so close to the viewer. He owned several skulls and returned to them in oil and watercolour in his final decade at Aix.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-the-mu: A violent scene in which two figures pin a third to the ground beside a body of water under a heavy sky. Oil on canvas, 64 by 81 cm, painted around 1870 and held by the Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool, under inventory WAG 6242. It belongs to the dark, dramatic subjects of Cézanne's early years.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-young-: A young woman in a striped blouse leans on a fabric-covered table, her head resting in her hand. Oil on canvas of about 1895 to 1900, accession 99.PA.40 in the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles. Cézanne built her bulk from broad blocks of colour while the space behind her shifts and tilts.
collection-of-beauty-paul-de-vos-bull-su: A bull-baiting scene of the kind de Vos perfected in Rubens's Antwerp circle, with mastiffs lunging at a tethered bull's flanks. The diagonal tangle of muscle, horn and fang demonstrates the Flemish taste for animal combats as showcases of anatomical drama and tonal bravura.
collection-of-beauty-paul-de-vos-cats-fi: A pantry overturned by brawling cats among hanging game, fish and copper vessels, a kitchen-piece genre popularized by Frans Snyders and continued by his brother-in-law de Vos. The hissing animals serve as a moralized emblem of greed and chaos disrupting domestic order.
collection-of-beauty-paul-de-vos-jan-wil: A Flemish Baroque collaboration in which Jan Wildens supplied the wooded paradise landscape and Paul de Vos populated it with the assembled animals of creation. Such division of labor was standard practice in Antwerp's specialist workshops, here producing a dense menagerie set within a luminous park-like clearing.
collection-of-beauty-paul-de-vos-still-l: A monumental Flemish pronk still life heaped with fruit, game and silver, attended by a servant figure likely contributed by a collaborating figure painter. The composition exemplifies the Antwerp specialty of combining a Snyders-school animal painter with a portraitist for sumptuous decorative ensembles.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-001: An academic life study from Gauguin's early years, predating the Tahitian primitivism for which he is now remembered. The figure is modelled with conventional tonal shading, evidence of the studio training he would soon discard for synthetism.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-004: Annah, the thirteen-year-old Javanese model Gauguin took in on his return to Paris, sits naked in a blue armchair with a small monkey at her feet. Painted in the Rue Vercingétorix studio in 1893 or 1894, the canvas carries the Tahitian inscription Aita tamari vahine Judith te parari and now hangs in the Stavros Niarchos collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-018-th: A boy in blue tends a herd of black and pink pigs across a hillside above a Breton village, the field divided into flat zones of red, ochre and green. Painted at Pont-Aven in late 1888, the canvas was acquired by Norton Simon and shows Gauguin moving from broken Impressionist touch toward the cloisonnist patches of flat colour outlined in dark contour.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-036: Four Breton peasant women in white coifs and dark dresses lean over a low fence in conversation, a man ploughing with geese in the upper distance. Gauguin painted the canvas at Pont-Aven in 1886 during his first Breton summer, catalogued W.201 in the Wildenstein corpus; it now belongs to the Bayerische Staatsgemaeldesammlungen on deposit at the Neue Pinakothek in Munich.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-040: Vahine no te tiare, a young Tahitian woman in a high-collared mission dress, holds a single white gardenia at her chest. Gauguin's first Polynesian portrait, painted in 1891 and now in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, casts the sitter against a yellow ground patterned with red blossoms.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-044: Tahitian women in striped cotton dresses doze on the veranda of a thatched hut, one ironing while a child watches at the edge of the floor. Painted between 1892 and 1894 during Gauguin's first stay in Tahiti, the canvas was owned successively by Edgar Degas and Walter Annenberg before entering the Metropolitan Museum.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-056: Two Tahitian women in pareu sit on the sand at the edge of a brilliant turquoise lagoon, one in profile, the other facing forward with hands folded in her lap. Painted during Gauguin's first Tahitian sojourn of 1891-1893, the canvas flattens beach, sea, and sky into bands of saturated colour and now hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-059: A snow-covered Paris garden seen from the window, the bare branches and low wall reduced to muted whites, blues and umbers. Gauguin painted the small canvas in 1879, still a stockbroker and Sunday painter under Camille Pissarro's tutelage; it now hangs in the Budapest Museum of Fine Arts.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-072: Marie Ginoux sits at a marble café table in Arles with a green absinthe glass and a soda siphon, while a billiard table and a row of slumped drinkers fill the back of the room. Painted in early November 1888 during Gauguin's two months sharing the Yellow House with Van Gogh, the canvas was acquired by the Pushkin Museum in Moscow from the Shchukin collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-085: A view of the ancient Roman necropolis at Arles, painted during Gauguin's stay with Van Gogh in autumn 1888. The avenue of stone sarcophagi recedes between flame-orange trees, the foreground simplified into broad zones of saturated color that anticipate the cloisonnist style.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-087: An early Martinique canvas from Gauguin's 1887 stay near Saint-Pierre, showing local women gathering fruit beneath dense tropical foliage. Painted before his Tahitian voyages, the work already shows his shift away from Impressionist brushwork toward flatter, decorative arrangements of figure and landscape.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-090: Three Tahitian women rest on the shore in long pareu, a band of pink sand cutting horizontally across the picture between sea and palm-shadowed earth. Painted in 1899, the canvas belongs to Gauguin's late Tahitian phase in which figures sit motionless within broad blocks of saturated colour.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-091: A nude Tahitian woman lies across a bed in shadowed interior light, watched by a black bird perched on the sill while two figures murmur in the doorway. Gauguin painted Nevermore in 1897 and titled it after Poe's raven; the canvas now hangs in the Courtauld Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-105: Five riders move across a pink-purple beach on Hiva Oa, two leading figures wearing the conical hooded shroud Gauguin associated with Breton funerals. The first of two versions painted in 1902, this canvas was acquired by Karl Ernst Osthaus from Vollard for the Museum Folkwang in Essen.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-106: Five horsemen pass along a Marquesan beach under a low sky, the lavender sand pulling the figures forward in a flat, decorative frieze. The second of two versions Gauguin painted in 1902 on Hiva Oa, the canvas later entered the Stavros Niarchos Collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-110: Gauguin, gaunt and bearded in a yellow shirt, sets his own head against a flat green ground inscribed près du Golgotha. Painted in Tahiti in 1896 during a period of illness and debt, the self-portrait casts the artist as suffering Christ; the canvas is in the Museu de Arte de São Paulo.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-112: Gauguin paints himself in the role of Hugo's outlaw Jean Valjean, gaunt-cheeked against a wallpaper of pink flowers, with a small portrait of Émile Bernard pinned behind him. Sent to Vincent van Gogh in Arles in autumn 1888 as part of the exchange of self-portraits among the Pont-Aven group, the canvas now belongs to the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-113: Mahana no atua, painted in Paris between Gauguin's two Tahitian sojourns, presents an idol of the moon goddess Hina flanked by ritual bathers. The lower foreground dissolves into pools of pure, mirror-bright color, an experiment in flat decorative abstraction that would influence Nabi and Fauve painters.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-121: A still life arranges a sculpted self-portrait jug, a folded coloured cloth and a Japanese woodcut tacked to the wall behind. Painted in Paris in winter 1889 after Gauguin's return from Pont-Aven, the canvas combines his interest in primitive ceramic forms with the ukiyo-e prints then circulating among the Pont-Aven and Nabis painters.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-1880-t: Gauguin's wife Mette Sophie sits at a small table bent over her sewing, the dense brushwork drawn from Camille Pissarro's example. The 116 by 81 cm canvas, painted in 1880 while Gauguin was still a successful stockbroker, hangs at the Foundation E. G. Bührle in Zurich and is catalogued as Wildenstein 65.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-200: Gauguin, in his late twenties and still a Paris stockbroker, looks out from beneath a soft toque in muted browns and greys. Painted around 1875 to 1877, the small canvas is the earliest known self-portrait of an artist whose face would become one of the most painted subjects in his late Polynesian work; it is in the Harvard Art Museums.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-contes: Two young Tahitian women sit in a flowering grove while a crouching red-haired devil, an exaggerated likeness of the Dutch painter Meyer de Haan, lurks behind them. Painted in 1902 on Hiva Oa and now at the Museum Folkwang in Essen, the picture revisits Gauguin's old Pont-Aven companion as a demonic figure shadowing his Marquesan paradise.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-d-ou-v: A sleeping infant, a youth picking fruit, and an old woman crouched beside a blue idol stretch across nearly four metres of Tahitian forest. Gauguin painted the canvas in late 1897 as an intended summation before a suicide attempt, and it now anchors the collection of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-deux-t: Two bare-breasted Tahitian women stand close in the picture plane, one holding a tray of mango blossoms. Gauguin painted the canvas in 1899 in Punaauia and it entered the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1949 as part of the William Church Osborn gift.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-l-espr: Front and back covers of Gauguin's handwritten 1902 manuscript L'Esprit Moderne et le Catholicisme, with watercolour and gouache decoration of Tahitian figures and ornamental script. Written on Hiva Oa near the end of his life, the polemical text attacked the Catholic mission's authority over the Marquesans, an argument that earned Gauguin a libel conviction shortly before his death.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-la-ber: A young shepherdess sits barefoot on the grass with her flock in a sloping Pont-Aven pasture, the village rooftops in the middle distance. Gauguin signed and dated the canvas P Gauguin 86 at lower left, among the first works of his initial Brittany summer; it entered the Laing Art Gallery in Newcastle as a gift from the National Art Collections Fund in 1945.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-le-par: A nude couple stand among heavy tropical foliage, the woman reaching toward fruit while a serpent threads the branches behind. Painted around 1890 in Brittany and now at the Yale University Art Gallery, the canvas anticipates the Edenic imagery Gauguin would rework after his first voyage to Tahiti in 1891.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-le-sor: A long-haired Marquesan in a short blue tunic and red cape stands frontally with a dog and bird at his feet, two veiled women shrinking behind a tree. Painted on Hiva Oa in 1902 and now at the Musée d'Art moderne in Liège, the figure is based on Haapuani, a local healer Gauguin had befriended in his final years.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-manao-: A nude Tahitian girl, Gauguin's young companion Teha'amana, lies face down on a yellow bed while an old woman in a hood sits watching from the foot of the frame. Painted in oil on burlap in 1892 and now in the Albright-Knox Art Gallery, the title refers to the tupapau, Polynesian spirits believed to haunt the night.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-self-p: Gauguin sets his bespectacled face against a pale background, the gaze steady and the body shrunken by illness in the final months on Hiva Oa. The last known self-portrait, painted in 1903 and now at the Kunstmuseum Basel, was reaffirmed as autograph by the museum after technical analysis in 2025.

Gauguin stares out from a flat red and yellow ground, a green snake coiling in one hand, three ripe apples floating beside his head and a thin golden halo above. Painted on a cupboard door at the Le Pouldu inn in 1889 and now at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the picture casts the artist as a sardonic Eden serpent and Christian saint at once.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-tahiti: A standing Tahitian woman in a white gown turns from a small dark tupapau figure crouched at the right edge, the colours pitched to flat reds, ochres and violet. Gauguin worked the canvas around 1899 in Punaauia, reworking the spirit-of-the-dead motif he had first painted in Manao tupapau seven years earlier.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-te-aa-: A young Tahitian woman sits nude on a patterned cloth, holding a sprouting mango seed against a field of flowering shrubs. Gauguin painted Te aa no areois, the Seed of the Areoi, in 1892 during his first Tahitian stay, casting his model Teha'amana as the mythic ancestress of the Areoi religious society; the canvas is now in MoMA.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-two-wo: A young Tahitian girl leans against an older woman in red against a flowering ground, the heads close together in quiet attention. Painted in 1899 in Punaauia, the canvas entered the Metropolitan Museum of Art through the Walter H. Annenberg collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gustave-dore-a: Gustave Dore's vision of Andromeda, the Ethiopian princess chained to a sea cliff awaiting Perseus's rescue. The composition exploits Dore's signature contrast of luminous flesh against turbulent rock and sky, a Romantic theatricality refined through years of book illustration. This file represents a digitally restored version of the image.
collection-of-beauty-paul-klee-1922-sene: A stylised head built from concentric planes of yellow, orange and red, the eyes asymmetrical, one circular and one almond-shaped. Painted in oil on chalk-primed gauze in 1922, the panel was acquired by the Kunstmuseum Basel in 1931 and so escaped Nazi confiscation. Klee made it during his Bauhaus years in Weimar, where he was pushing colour theory toward geometric reduction.
collection-of-beauty-paul-klee-invention: A gaunt naked woman lies wedged into the bare branches of a tree, her elongated body rendered in sharp etched line. Plate 3 of the Inventionen series, the 1903 etching was printed in Bern by Max Girardet in an edition of about sixty and entered MoMA's collection in 1941 after being purged from German museums as degenerate art.
collection-of-beauty-peasant-family-goin: A peasant strides ahead on foot, laden with his gear, leading the horse on which his wife rides with a small child clinging on behind her; the road winds past a rocky crag toward a village with a church in the distance. One of Schongauer's secular genre engravings, it treats everyday rural life with the same fineness of line as his devotional prints. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-pedro-pablo-rubens-: Susanna twists away from two leering elders who press in from the shadows of her garden bath, her startled body and rumpled drapery filling the canvas. Painted shortly after Rubens's return from Italy, the picture fuses Venetian colour with the muscular Roman figures he had studied there.
collection-of-beauty-peinturesmuseefabre: Venus leans toward Vulcan in his forge to plead for arms for her son Aeneas, the Cyclopes labouring at the anvil behind. Submitted as the painter's morceau de réception to the Académie Royale in 1734, the picture is a polished demonstration of the decorative Rococo mythology Natoire would soon deploy at Versailles.
collection-of-beauty-pellegrinibydegas: Carlo Pellegrini, the Italian-born caricaturist who signed his Vanity Fair plates as Ape, is shown three-quarter length in a soft hat and overcoat. Worked in mixed watercolour, oil and pastel on paper around 1876 to 1877 and inscribed à vous, the sheet was Degas's return present after Pellegrini had painted him in London; it is in the National Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-persus-and-andromed: Perseus swoops on his winged horse toward the chained Andromeda while the sea monster thrashes in the surf below. Wtewael, a leading Utrecht Mannerist, paints the nude princess against a rocky Mediterranean shore where her parents kneel in prayer, the composition built from the elongated figures and porcelain skin typical of his late style.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-ruben-s-: Four mounted soldiers strain over the standard of Anghiari, mouths open and horses crashing teeth-to-teeth in the central fight. Drawn around 1603 after Leonardo's lost mural for the Palazzo della Signoria, the sheet is the most authoritative surviving record of the composition Vasari painted over around 1560.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-0: Bathsheba sits at her bath while a black page delivers David's letter, the Old Testament narrative reframed as an excuse for sumptuous flesh, drapery, and still life. The painting now hangs in the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Dresden.

Salome presents the head of John the Baptist on a salver as Herod recoils at the banquet table. Rubens stages the gruesome moment with theatrical lighting and a dense crush of guests, balancing horror against the gleam of silver and silk.

An intimate, near-life-size portrait of Rubens's second wife Helena Fourment, draped only in a fur cloak. The picture's frank sensuality and tender naturalism mark it as a private image, kept in the artist's own household.

A panoramic view of the country estate Rubens purchased in 1635, with its turreted manor set among golden Brabant fields. The artist treats native landscape with vigorous brushwork and a low, glowing horizon, anticipating later Romantic vistas.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-1: Paris awards the golden apple to Venus while Juno and Minerva recoil in defeat, their nudes arranged in a graceful triad against an Arcadian landscape. Rubens revisited this mythological subject several times; the late Prado version is among his most assured.

A formal portrait of the young Mantuan duke Vincenzo II Gonzaga, painted during Rubens's years at the Gonzaga court. Lace, armour, and the sitter's pale gaze are rendered with the courtly polish the artist absorbed from Italian models.

From the Decius Mus cycle, a tapestry-cartoon-scale battle scene in which the Roman consul plunges to his ritual death amid rearing horses and clashing standards. The composition is a swirling diagonal of armoured bodies, an early showcase of Rubensian dynamism.

A state portrait of Isabella of Bourbon, queen consort of Spain, in stiff black court dress and pearls. Rubens softens the rigid Habsburg formula with subtle modelling of the face and a discreet warmth in the flesh tones.

Hercules grapples the invulnerable Nemean lion in a knot of straining limbs, the hero's first labor reduced to its essential close-quarters violence. The Apsley House version follows a Rubens prototype that translates antique sculptural sources, especially the Belvedere Torso, into Baroque flesh and sinew.

A bust-length portrait of a bearded gentleman in the stiff white ruff fashionable in early seventeenth-century Antwerp. The Colchester picture is an after-Rubens version, its frontal pose and economical handling typical of workshop replicas produced for civic and merchant patrons.

Cain raises a jawbone-club above his fallen brother in a violent, sculpturally compressed composition modelled on Michelangelo's Sistine ignudi. The Courtauld panel is a small but ferocious meditation on humanity's first murder, its diagonal locked into the surface like a relief.

Christ confers the keys of binding and loosing on Saint Peter, the foundational image of papal primacy revived for Counter-Reformation polemic. Rubens isolates the two figures against an open sky, emphasizing the gesture's solemnity and the apostle's age-roughened hands.

A workshop-tradition Madonna and Child in which the Virgin cradles a robust infant Christ against a dark ground. The composition follows one of Rubens's many devotional formulas, refined in his Antwerp shop for export across Catholic Europe.

Diana and her companions recoil from leering satyrs at a forest pool in a late mythological invention treating chastity disturbed. Rubens entrusted much of the landscape and animal staffage to specialist collaborators, while reserving the warm, dimpled female nudes for himself.

The huntress goddess in red, drawing back her bow as hounds drive a stag through dense woodland. The picture belongs to Rubens's late series of aristocratic chase subjects, where landscape, animals and figure painting were typically distributed among studio specialists.

An oil head study, painted directly from a Antwerp model, of the kind Rubens kept on file for reuse as apostles, philosophers and patriarchs in larger compositions. The rapid wet-into-wet handling and ruddy flesh tones show his working method at its most direct.

The sea-god enthrones his Nereid bride amid a tumult of tritons, sea-horses and rolling waves. Rubens treats the marine pageantry as a fleshy Baroque counterpart to ancient sea-thiasos sarcophagi, the muscular Neptune contrasted with Amphitrite's pearly skin.

A bust portrait of an aged sitter in dark robes and a white collar, his face recorded with the unsentimental specificity of Rubens's mature portraiture. Studies of this kind doubled as preparatory material for biblical and historical figures requiring weathered authority.

A school-of-Rubens Lamentation in which the dead Christ is supported by Mary, John and the holy women in a tightly knit pyramid of grief. The piled drapery and waxen flesh follow patterns Rubens established in altarpieces for Antwerp's churches after his return from Italy.

The Carmelite reformer kneels in ecstasy as the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, an episode central to her Vida and to Counter-Reformation devotional propaganda. Rubens renders the moment as a swift, fluid oil sketch built around upward-spiralling drapery and light.

The drunken tutor of Bacchus staggers forward, supported by satyrs and maenads in a frieze of overripe flesh, grapes and laughter. Rubens treats Silenus as a Christianized parable of intemperance, the figures drawn from antique sources but warmed by Venetian color.

The Carmelite mystic kneels in ecstasy as Christ appears in a burst of golden cloud. Rubens treats the Counter-Reformation visionary subject with operatic light and surging drapery, in keeping with the Jesuit altarpieces of his Antwerp years.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-2: A bust-length likeness of an unidentified gentleman in dark dress with a starched white collar. The directness of the gaze and the economical handling of the flesh suggest a private commission painted in the artist's mature Antwerp studio.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-a: Rubens's homage to Titian, copied during his stay in Madrid where he studied the royal collection. The serpent-child reaches down to Eve as Adam grasps her arm; Rubens warms the Venetian palette and softens the contours toward his own fleshier ideal.

Shepherds press in around the manger, faces lit from below by the Christ child as Mary draws back the cloth. The diagonal massing of figures and theatrical lighting reflect Rubens's recent absorption of Caravaggio during his Italian years.

An ecorche drawing exposing the muscles of the male torso and limbs, made for the artist's own study of human structure. Such sheets fed the powerfully built figures of his history paintings and were later engraved as a teaching aid.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-c: The first murder rendered as violent close-quarters struggle, Cain's club raised above his fallen brother. Rubens compresses the action into a tight pyramidal group, exploiting contorted limbs and chiaroscuro for moral force.

The apostle is shown crucified upside down at his own request, his contorted, foreshortened body filling a tall altarpiece format. Commissioned for St Peter's Church in Cologne, the work was among the artist's last major altarpieces, completed shortly before his death and dispatched to the parish where his father had once lived.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-d: A small child, often identified as Rubens's nephew Philip, looks out from a softly lit ground while gently holding a bird in one hand. The intimate scale and warm flesh tones place the panel within the painter's family portraits, a private counterpart to the grand commissions for which he is better known.

A monumental Saint Jerome at his desk, lion at his feet, translating the Vulgate by lamplight. Rubens emphasizes the hermit-scholar's powerful aged anatomy and the deep red drapery of the cardinal, a saint frequently invoked in Counter-Reformation imagery as a model of biblical orthodoxy.

Painted on the outer wing of the Antwerp Cathedral triptych, this panel forms part of one of the central Counter-Reformation altarpieces of the Low Countries. The weight of Christ's body, lowered along a white shroud, anchors a tightly knit group of mourners.

Diana and her companions, returning from the hunt with hounds and game, are accosted by lecherous satyrs at the edge of a wood. The collision of nude bodies, fur and dead quarry typifies Rubens's late mythological mode.

The huntress goddess strides forward with her nymphs, bow in hand and hounds at her heels, fresh game slung from her shoulder. The composition celebrates the chase as a pretext for studies of the female nude in motion.

The Stoic philosopher stands in a basin while a physician opens his veins, his upturned head and outstretched arms recalling the antique sculpture Rubens had drawn in Rome. The picture distills the Baroque taste for Stoic exemplars of virtuous death.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-e: A peasant cart laden with felled timber rumbles down a rutted track as the day's last light catches clouds and treetops. The naturalistic Flemish countryside and warm low sun place this among the personal landscapes Rubens painted for his own pleasure.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-f: The Titan, chained to a Caucasian crag, writhes as the eagle of Zeus tears at his liver in a horizontal composition Rubens developed with Frans Snyders, who painted the bird. The torsion of the body shows Rubens's debt to Michelangelo and the Laocoön, fused with North-Italian colorism. Rubens treated the subject at least twice: this Philadelphia Museum of Art canvas is the autograph version begun around 1611, and a second autograph version (c. 1613) survives at the Landesmuseum Oldenburg.

Venus and her attendants strip the war-god of his armor while putti tug at his weapons, an allegory of love's pacifying power over violence. Painted in collaboration with Jan Brueghel the Elder, who supplied the rich still life of arms, garlands and shimmering accoutrements.

Four oil sketches of the same Black sitter, observed from different angles and in varied light, made as working material for finished compositions including the Adoration of the Magi. The studies are notable for their direct, dignified attention to an individual model.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-h: Mary, the infant Christ, Joseph and the young Saint John gather in a domestic interior with a parrot perched nearby, a bird traditionally read as a symbol of the Virgin's purity. The warmly lit grouping shows Rubens reworking a Renaissance devotional formula in his own fleshy idiom.

An allegorical Hercules, club raised, tramples a writhing female personification of Discord underfoot. The image was conceived as a ceiling design celebrating princely virtue triumphing over civil strife.
Hercules wraps the invulnerable lion in a strangling embrace, the hero's bunched muscles answered by the beast's twisting flank. The motif derives from antique sarcophagi Rubens had studied in Italy.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-i: Rubens's first wife is portrayed in the guise of Glycera, the ancient Greek flower seller, garlanded and surrounded by blooms. The conceit fuses tender domestic likeness with classical learning.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-j: Judith holds aloft the severed head of the Assyrian general while her maidservant looks on in the half-dark of the tent. Rubens treats the Old Testament heroine with the heightened drama and tactile flesh of his early Italianate manner.

A bust-length portrait of a young man in a black flat cap, copied after a sixteenth-century original by the Antwerp painter Willem Key. The grave, even lighting and restrained palette preserve the sober character of the Northern Renaissance prototype.

Juno gathers the hundred eyes of the slain giant Argus from his severed head and sets them into the tail of her peacock. The Ovidian subject is staged as a brilliantly coloured open-air tableau of nymphs, birds and rich textiles.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-k: A bound and crowned Christ is presented to the crowd, his torso lit against a brooding ground in the manner Rubens used to dramatize Passion scenes. The taut musculature and fall of light over the shoulders intensify the Counter-Reformation appeal to compassion.

A spare, intimate Lamentation in which the Virgin and Saint John bend over Christ's pale body laid against a darkened ground. Rubens reduces the cast to its essential mourners, concentrating Counter-Reformation devotional intensity in the contrast of cool flesh and ash-gray drapery.

An allegory of the four continents personified as river gods reclining beside their female consorts, traditionally identified with the Danube, Nile, Ganges and Rio de la Plata. Tigers, a crocodile and lush vegetation underscore the cosmographic ambition of the Vienna canvas.

A storm-drenched Ovidian landscape in which Jupiter and Mercury, sheltered by the pious Philemon and Baucis, unleash a deluge upon the surrounding valley. The boiling sky, falling trees and rain-swollen torrent show Rubens absorbing Venetian and Adam Elsheimer landscape models for cosmic moral drama.

Bishop Ambrose bars Emperor Theodosius from Milan Cathedral after the massacre at Thessalonica, a Counter-Reformation parable of clerical authority over secular power. Rubens stages the confrontation on the church steps with massed retinues, reworking a composition first treated by his Venetian model Veronese.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-l: The dead Christ lies on a sheaf of straw, mourned by the Virgin, John and the Marys at the foot of the Cross. The pallid body, sharply foreshortened, recalls Rubens's debt to Italian models of the Pieta.

A nocturnal Lamentation in which torchlight rakes across Christ's body and the bowed faces of his mourners. The compressed grouping and dark surround intensify the emotional pitch in the Italianate Baroque manner.

A broad Flemish countryside opens out under a sky cleared by a passing storm, a rainbow arching over fields, milkmaids and grazing cattle. Often paired with the View of Het Steen, it expresses Rubens's late identification with the land around his country house.

Roman ruins on the Palatine hill rise above figures and herds in a panoramic landscape conceived from sketches made during the artist's years in Italy. Antiquity is set in dialogue with a fertile, lived-in countryside.

Christ raises the bread at the centre of the long table while the apostles react in agitation; Judas turns toward the viewer with averted eyes. The picture concentrates on the moment of institution rather than the announcement of betrayal, in line with Counter-Reformation Eucharistic devotion.

Inside a shadowed rocky grotto, Lot's two daughters ply their elderly father with wine, the burning city of Sodom glowing in the distance. The compact, candle-lit composition is typical of Rubens's early Antwerp years, when Caravaggesque tenebrism still inflected his treatment of biblical narrative.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-m: The Virgin is borne aloft by a swirl of angels while the apostles cluster around her empty tomb below. The upward spiralling composition is a hallmark of Rubens's altarpieces for the Antwerp churches of the early seventeenth century.

Mercury, sent by Jupiter, lulls the hundred-eyed guardian Argus to sleep with his pipes before drawing his sword. The Ovidian story is staged in a wooded landscape with the white heifer Io tethered to one side.

Moses raises the bronze serpent on a pole as stricken Israelites writhe in the foreground, their wounds healed at a glance. The crowded, twisting figures provide a typological prefiguration of the Crucifixion familiar in Counter-Reformation imagery.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-n: A red chalk drawing of the painter's young son, his round face and tousled hair caught with the directness of family observation. Such intimate studies of his children are among the most personal works in Rubens's draughtsmanship.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-o: An aged woman shields a candle flame as a boy leans in to light his own taper from hers, the two faces modelled by the small light source. The picture belongs to the Northern tradition of nocturnal genre studies descending from Caravaggio and the Bassano workshop.

An aged peasant woman bent beneath a heavy basket of coal, her weathered face caught in firelit chiaroscuro. Painted in Rubens's late manner, the unsentimental study of labor and age departs from his courtly subjects, prizing physiognomic truth and tactile flesh.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-p: Perseus, fresh from slaying the sea-monster, unbinds the nude Andromeda as putti and Pegasus crowd the rocky shore. The composition pairs heroic male armor with luminous female flesh in a swirling Baroque celebration of rescue and erotic deliverance.

The apostle Peter, instructed by Christ to pay the Temple tax, retrieves a silver coin from a fish's mouth (Matthew 17:27). Rubens stages the miracle as a robust half-length figure study, the fisherman's tanned forearms and concentrated gaze given Caravaggesque weight.

An intimate likeness of the artist's daughter Clara Serena, who died at twelve, her round cheeks flushed and chestnut hair loosely brushed. The brisk, affectionate handling, more sketch than commission, ranks among the most tender child portraits of the seventeenth century.

The German Catholic polemicist Kaspar Schoppe sits at his writing table, pen in hand, returning the viewer's gaze with scholarly directness. Painted during Rubens's Italian years, the portrait fuses Venetian color with the sober psychological scrutiny of Northern humanist likenesses.

The Genoese-born Habsburg general Ambrogio Spinola, victor at Breda, appears in burnished black armor with a crisp lace collar and the red sash of command. Rubens, who knew the marquess personally during the Twelve Years' Truce, distills authority into a steady, weary gaze.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-s: Saint Francis of Assisi kneels in ecstatic communion, his gaunt features and brown habit picked out against a darkened ground. The economy of means and devotional intensity reflect Counter-Reformation taste for affective images of penitent saints.

A workshop image of Democritus, the Greek thinker known in antiquity as the laughing philosopher, mocking the follies of humankind. His broad smile and weathered features draw on the Northern tradition of philosopher portraits revived by Rubens and his circle.

The painter, near sixty, presents himself in broad-brimmed hat, sword, and gloves — courtier and diplomat as much as artist. The dignified late self-portrait, withholding palette and brushes, asserts his ennoblement and standing among Europe's rulers.

The drunken satyr Silenus, tutor of Bacchus, lurches forward supported by his bacchic retinue, his bloated torso pinkly luminous against shadow. Rubens revisits the antique theme with characteristic relish for unidealized flesh and the comic gravity of intoxication.

Silenus sprawls in heavy slumber while satyrs, nymphs and a leopard wreath him with grapes in a leafy clearing. Painted soon after Rubens's return from Italy, the canvas distills Bacchic mythology into a pulsing arrangement of intertwined nudes and animal life.

An oil study of the crucified Christ, the body arched against the cross with head fallen onto the right shoulder. Rubens prepared the figure for one of his Antwerp altarpieces around 1610, working out the torsion of the muscles in rapid, ruddy brushwork on panel before scaling the design up to full size.

An oil sketch of a bearded male head, turned in three-quarter view and lit from above. Such tronies served as workshop reference for apostles and biblical elders, and show Rubens's quick, fluent brushwork unburdened by narrative finish.

A personification of Summer as harvest and abundance, with peasants gathering grain beneath a glowing sky. Part of a seasonal cycle, the image links rural labor to Flemish landscape tradition and to Rubens's late absorption in country life at Het Steen.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-t: Saint Peter holds the keys of the Kingdom, his furrowed brow and grizzled beard rendered with apostolic gravitas. An early work in Rubens's Apostolado tradition, the figure typifies the half-length devotional saint favored by Counter-Reformation patrons.

The infant Hercules, set to Juno's breast by Jupiter, draws milk so forcefully that the spilled stream becomes the Milky Way. Painted for Philip IV's Torre de la Parada, the canvas turns an Ovidian etiology into a swirl of cosmic drapery and divine flesh.

Moses raises the bronze serpent on a pole as Israelites writhe with snakebites below, looking up to be healed (Numbers 21). Rubens packs the foreground with anatomical contortions, a Counter-Reformation allegory of salvation through faith in the Crucified.

Venus rushes to the dying Adonis as he collapses beside the boar that has gored him, while putti mourn and his hounds bay. The sweeping diagonal of the lovers' bodies and the velvet handling of flesh against thunderous sky exemplify Rubens's mature Ovidian manner.

The lifeless Christ is lowered from the cross into the arms of the mourning Virgin and disciples, his pale flesh contrasted with the deep crimson of Joseph of Arimathea's robe. An early Roman-period work, it absorbs lessons from Caravaggio and the Carracci.

Muscular soldiers heave the cross upright on a steep diagonal, Christ's luminous body twisting against a stormy sky. Conceived for Antwerp's St. Walburga, the great triptych translates Italian heroic anatomy into a Flemish altarpiece of unprecedented physical force.

Christ's body is lowered onto the slab of anointing as the Marys and disciples crowd in grief. Rubens tightens Caravaggio's Vatican prototype into an oval of mourning figures, the dead flesh phosphorescent against the surrounding shadow.

Phaeton plummets from the chariot of the Sun as Jupiter's thunderbolt scatters the bolting horses and the Hours recoil through the zodiac. An early mythological tour de force, the picture shows Rubens already pushing Mannerist motion toward Baroque theater.

Worshippers garland a statue of Venus while putti, nymphs and satyrs dance in pagan revelry. Inspired by Titian's Worship of Venus and a passage in Philostratus, the late composition assembles Rubens's lifelong vocabulary of mythic celebration.

An aged hermit, drawn from Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, gazes lasciviously upon the sleeping Angelica in a moonlit forest. Rubens contrasts ascetic gauntness with luminous female flesh, transforming the chivalric romance into a Baroque meditation on temptation.

The Trojan prince Paris weighs the golden apple between Juno, Minerva and Venus while Mercury looks on. An early version of a subject Rubens revisited often, the composition arranges three nude goddesses to display Italianate disegno absorbed during his stay in Rome.

The Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier raises the dead and heals the afflicted before a toppling pagan idol, the converted crowding toward him in awe. Painted for Antwerp's Jesuit church, the altarpiece celebrates the global reach of Counter-Reformation evangelism.

Straining executioners heave the cross bearing Christ skyward in a violent diagonal of muscular labor. A late reprise of his Antwerp altarpiece, this version concentrates the drama into a tighter, more urgent gathering of bodies and tackle.

The Phoenician princess clings to the white bull-Jupiter as he wades into the sea bound for Crete, while companions wave helplessly from shore. Painted as a copy after Titian for Philip IV, the canvas pays homage to Venetian color while asserting Rubens's own touch.

Christ hangs between the two thieves, the crosses set against a darkening sky in a tightly massed composition. Rubens compresses the Calvary scene into a vertical screen of straining bodies, a Counter-Reformation meditation on suffering and redemption.

Venus admires herself in a mirror held by a winged Cupid, a maidservant arranging her golden hair. The intimate composition, drawn from Titian's prototypes, balances cool reflective surface against the warm pink expanse of the goddess's back.

The Madonna and Child appear within an exuberant wreath of blossoms, painted in collaboration with the flower specialist Jan Brueghel the Elder. The conceit fuses Marian devotion with Antwerp's expertise in still life, the garland a votive offering of created beauty.

Two satyrs, one with a clutch of grapes and a piercing forward stare, the other grinning behind him, appear in close half-length view. The double tronie distills Rubens's vision of bacchic appetite into an arresting pair of bestial yet humanly knowing faces.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-v: Venus clings to the departing Adonis as he shoulders his spear and his hounds strain toward the fatal hunt. Rubens reworks Titian's Prado composition, heightening the embrace into a Baroque farewell of foreboding and tender resistance.

Rubens's own country estate near Mechelen lies under a low, golden dawn, with a hunter, hay wagon and far-flung fields stretching to the horizon. The expansive panorama, painted for personal pleasure, helped redirect Northern landscape toward atmospheric naturalism.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-w: An oil study of an armoured soldier, executed with the loose brushwork and ruddy palette Rubens reserved for working sketches. The figure's head and gleaming breastplate are modelled with rapid, confident strokes, capturing the swagger of a Baroque military type.

A half-length nude turns toward a mirror held by a maid, her pearly flesh rendered in the warm, fluid manner of Rubens's late period. The composition belongs to a Venetian-derived tradition of the toilette of Venus, transformed here by Flemish opulence.
collection-of-beauty-petergansevoortbyst: Peter Gansevoort, the defender of Fort Stanwix in 1777, wears the dark blue coat and gold epaulettes of a Continental general. Stuart painted the portrait in 1794, around the time Gansevoort was commissioned brigadier general of the New York militia; the canvas is now at the Munson-Williams-Proctor Arts Institute in Utica.
collection-of-beauty-philipp-otto-runge-: A portrait of the painter and writer Friedrich August von Klinkowström, Runge's close friend and a fellow figure in early German Romantic circles. The sitter is shown with a Nazarene-like clarity of contour and a steady, contemplative gaze.

Three young siblings of the Hülsenbeck family stand and crouch in a Hamburg garden, the toddler clutching a sunflower leaf almost as large as himself. Runge invests the children with hieratic gravity, treating childhood as a metaphysical state.

A close study of a hound's head in chalk and lead, the breed's soft fur and alert eye observed with quiet precision. The drawing belongs to Runge's wider effort to ground his Romantic symbolism in patient natural observation.

Christ stretches out his hand to a sinking Peter on the Sea of Galilee, the figures reduced to clear, near-archaic outlines. Runge's interpretation of the Gospel episode reflects his ambition to fuse landscape, religion, and Romantic symbolism.

A black and white chalk drawing of the young Sophia Sieveking laid out in death, her features composed against a pale pillow. Runge made the sheet shortly before his own early death, lending its mortuary stillness an autobiographical weight.

A preparatory drawing in chalk and pencil for the unfinished Great Morning, mapping out the central goddess-figure rising amid lilies and infant spirits. The sheet shows Runge's diagrammatic approach to his cosmological Times of Day cycle.

A detail from the unfinished Great Morning, showing the radiant central figure Runge devised as the embodiment of dawn within his Times of Day cycle. The hard-edged drawing and saturated colour reveal the artist's mystical, almost emblematic Romanticism.
collection-of-beauty-picabia-hera-2: Three female faces float in superimposed contour against a ground of leaves and pale flowers, with the suggestion of a nude back behind them. Executed around 1929 in oil, gouache, charcoal and pencil on board at 103.4 by 74.9 cm, the picture belongs to Picabia's Transparencies series begun on the Riviera after his break with the Paris avant-garde.
collection-of-beauty-picabia-stardancer: A music-hall dancer dissolves into prismatic shards of pink and blue aboard a transatlantic steamer. Painted in 1913 on Picabia's voyage to New York for the Armory Show, the watercolour translates Cubist faceting into the chromatic energy he would soon name Orphism.
collection-of-beauty-picture-anger-of-th: Mountainous green waves pile over the deck of a foundering vessel under a thunderous sky, the hull listing as the crew loses control. Painted in 1886, the canvas belongs to Aivazovsky's late shipwreck series, in which the sea itself rather than any human protagonist becomes the antagonist of the scene.
collection-of-beauty-pierre-auguste-reno: A bust-length study of Gabrielle with her chemise slipped from one shoulder, the flesh rendered in warm pinks against a sketchy ground. The sitter is Gabrielle Renard, cousin of Renoir's wife Aline and the family's nanny from 1894, who modelled often in his later years. Painted about 1907, oil on canvas.

The Comédie-Française actress Jeanne Samary leans forward with parted lips and luminous eyes, her pink dress dissolving into the rosy ground. Renoir's brush builds the portrait almost entirely from warm, transparent layers of colour.

Ambroise Vollard leans over a small statuette of a kneeling nude, examining it as a connoisseur, his bald head and bulbous features softened by Renoir. The bronze is after the sculptor Aristide Maillol. Painted in 1908, oil on canvas, now in the Courtauld Gallery, London.

Charles and Georges Durand-Ruel, sons of Renoir's dealer, shown outdoors in three-piece suits against dense green foliage. Oil on canvas painted in 1882; Paul Durand-Ruel, who commissioned the double portrait, was reportedly displeased to find his sons painted out of doors. Charles holds a medallion, Georges a cigarette.

A double portrait of Renoir's friend the painter Alfred Sisley standing beside his companion, both in fashionable contemporary dress, the woman's arm through his. Painted in 1868 and now in the Wallraf-Richartz-Museum, Cologne, where it is catalogued as Das Ehepaar Sisley.

The art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel seated and contemplative, his dark coat set against a loosely brushed background. Durand-Ruel was the dealer who staked the Impressionists from the 1870s and a friend of Renoir for more than thirty years. Painted in 1910, oil on canvas.

The eight-year-old daughter of a Parisian banking family sits in profile, her copper hair flowing loose against a soft blue-green ground. Renoir's feathery brush captures both the child's reverie and the upholstered comfort of haute-bourgeois life.

A bust-length self-portrait with unkempt hair and beard, the painter in a striped shirt and dark tie against a loosely brushed ground. Renoir made it in 1875, oil on canvas, and showed it at the second Impressionist exhibition the following year; it is now in the Clark Art Institute, Williamstown.

A young woman in a straw hat leans by a sun-dappled lake, the foliage dissolved into iridescent strokes of green and pink. The picture exemplifies Renoir's sociable, plein-air Impressionism of the early 1880s.

Painted on the rocky beaches of Guernsey, where Renoir summered in 1883, the canvas shows small bathers playing among warm ochre boulders. The Channel light prompts a brighter, drier palette and the firmer drawing of his transitional period.

A couple dancing at an open-air ball, the woman in a red bonnet with a fan, a table of glasses behind them. Oil on canvas of 1883, Musée d'Orsay, Paris, paired with the contemporary Dance in the City. The models were Aline Charigot, later Renoir's wife, and his friend Paul Lhôte.

A nude woman holding a bow, a dead deer and an animal skin at her feet, cast as the huntress Diana. Oil on canvas, 197 by 132 cm, painted in 1867 and held by the National Gallery of Art, Washington. The model is thought to be Renoir's companion Lise Tréhot; the canvas was rejected by the 1867 Salon.

Renoir portrays his fellow Impressionist Frédéric Bazille at work before an easel, brush poised over a still life of a heron. The picture is a touching record of the early Batignolles circle, painted shortly before Bazille's death in the Franco-Prussian War.

A frieze of monumental nudes disports along a wooded bank, their crisp contours and pearly flesh marking Renoir's so-called Ingresque turn away from pure Impressionism. The picture occupied him for several years and now hangs at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

Renoir's son Jean, aged fifteen, poses full-length with a borrowed gun and the family dog Bob, dressed in a jacket his father thought suited a huntsman. Painted at Les Collettes in 1910, oil on canvas, about 173 by 89 cm. The sitter later became the filmmaker Jean Renoir; the canvas is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

Renoir's friends gather on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise at Chatou, lingering over wine and fruit after a row on the Seine. The composition weaves portraiture, still life, and shimmering river light into one celebrated image of modern leisure.

A wooded landscape at La Roche-Guyon, a village on a bend of the Seine in the Val-d'Oise. Oil on canvas painted in 1887, two years after Renoir had spent a summer there working alongside Cézanne. The picture is now in the Pérez Simón collection.

Robert Nunès in a sailor suit standing before a loosely brushed beach, his father the mayor of Yport on the Normandy coast. Oil on canvas painted in 1883, when Renoir was commissioned to portray the Nunès children, now in the Barnes Foundation, Philadelphia (BF325).

An early still life of garden flowers crowded into a white porcelain vase, painted under the influence of Courbet and Monet. The dense, dark ground and weighty paint surface show Renoir before his Impressionist palette had fully lightened.

Renoir's wife Aline stands with their eldest son Pierre, the young Jean held by a maid, and a neighbour's daughter gathered in front of a wall. Oil on canvas of 1896, catalogued BF819 in the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia. The painter set the figures close to the picture plane against a flatly brushed ground.

Renoir's view of Venice's central square dissolves the basilica's Byzantine facade into shimmering touches of pink, gold, and blue. Painted during his Italian journey, the canvas treats architecture as an Impressionist screen of light, with figures and pigeons scattered across the sunlit pavement.

A crowd under a canopy of umbrellas, a bare-headed milliner's assistant with her hatbox at the left edge. Renoir worked the canvas in two campaigns, the feathery right-hand figures about 1881 and the firmer left-hand pair around 1885, switching from cobalt to French ultramarine between them. Oil on canvas, National Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-pierre-cecile-puvis: A young traveller sleeps in a flowering meadow as three allegorical female figures, Love, Glory and Wealth, drift toward him through the dawn air. Puvis paints The Dream in the muted, fresco-like tonalities that made him a touchstone for the Symbolists.

An allegorical female nude personifying Hope sits on a barren battlefield, holding an olive branch as ruins and grave markers recede behind her. Painted in the aftermath of the Franco-Prussian War, the muted palette and frieze-like simplicity exemplify Puvis de Chavannes's pale, fresco-inspired symbolism.
collection-of-beauty-pierre-puvis-de-cha: A gaunt fisher stands in his moored skiff while a woman gathers flowers and an infant sleeps on the bank, the scene reduced to chalky, almost frescoed planes of pale color. The austere composition and melancholic mood made the picture a touchstone for Symbolist painters and the young Picasso.
collection-of-beauty-pieter-bruegel-d-a-: A teeming village square stages an allegorical joust between a barrel-riding Carnival, armed with a spit of meat, and a gaunt Lent on a church cart. Bruegel packs the panel with proverbs, Shrovetide revels, and Lenten almsgiving in a panoramic moral inventory of Netherlandish life.
collection-of-beauty-pieter-bruegel-der-: The Holy Family threads a precipitous mountain path while a vast world landscape opens beneath them, with rivers, cliffs, and a shadowed pagan idol toppling on a column. Bruegel's panoramic Weltlandschaft tradition dwarfs the sacred travelers within Alpine and Flemish topographies.
collection-of-beauty-pieter-bruegel-the-: A ploughman, shepherd, and angler go about their work along a sunlit harbor while Icarus's legs vanish almost unnoticed into the sea at lower right. The composition reads as a quiet meditation on Ovid's myth and human indifference, later memorialized in Auden's poem.

Soldiers ransack a snowbound Flemish village in a transposition of Herod's biblical slaughter into the contemporary Low Countries under Spanish occupation. In the Royal Collection version many of the slain children were overpainted as bundles, geese, and game by later hands.

A line of six blind men stumbles diagonally across the panel toward a ditch, each face individually studied for the disfigurements of disease. Bruegel illustrates Christ's parable from Matthew 15 with clinical precision and an unforgiving rhythm of falling bodies.

The smaller of Bruegel's two surviving Babel panels shows the spiraling brick ziggurat looming over a coastal plain, swallowed by storm clouds at its summit. Painstaking architectural detail draws on Roman ruins Bruegel had studied in Italy.

King Nimrod inspects stonemasons in the foreground as the colossal tower rises above a Flemish port, its arcades modeled on the Colosseum. The painting marries Genesis with a sober warning about overreaching ambition, rendered with engineering exactitude.
collection-of-beauty-pinacoteca-querini-: Cardinal Angelo Maria Querini in red moiré watered silk, holding a book in his Paduan study. Bartolomeo Nazari painted the Venetian-born cardinal and bibliophile around 1740; the portrait hangs in the Pinacoteca Querini Stampalia in Venice, founded on the family library Querini helped enlarge.
collection-of-beauty-plage-de-juan-les-p: From Monet's Antibes campaign on the Côte d'Azur, the canvas dissolves pines, sea and Alps into a high-keyed Mediterranean palette of pinks, mauves and turquoise. The artist complained the southern light was too bright to paint, yet returned with dozens of these luminous beach studies.
collection-of-beauty-plate-from-le-brun-: An engraved head demonstrates one of the expressions catalogued by Charles Le Brun in his 1668 lecture on the passions of the soul, drawn in red and brown ink. The plate comes from Carington Bowles's English edition published in London around 1785; the impression belongs to the Wellcome Collection.
collection-of-beauty-po-vodam-1888: Christ walks across a heaving green sea toward the disciples' boat, the figures of Peter stepping over the gunwale into the water. Aivazovsky painted the biblical scene in 1888, weaving his career-long marine vocabulary of luminous wave crests and storm light into a religious subject he returned to several times.
collection-of-beauty-polder-landscape-wi: Cattle wade through reedy lowland water beneath a wide Flemish sky, the herd dispersed across pasture and ditch. Rubens turned to such polder views in the late 1630s after retiring to his country estate at Het Steen.
collection-of-beauty-pont-argenteuil-mon: Sailing boats line the basin at Argenteuil beneath the highway bridge, their masts reflected in the broken blue water of the Seine. The picture belongs to the suburban riverscapes that defined the early Impressionist summers of 1872 to 1874.
collection-of-beauty-pont-neuf-1872-pier: Pedestrians and carriages cross Paris's oldest bridge under a clear summer sky, the Seine glittering between embankments. Renoir's brother Edmond reportedly delayed passersby in conversation so the painter could capture them in rapid, sun-drenched touches.
collection-of-beauty-pope-julius-ii: The aged della Rovere pope is seated in three-quarter view, beard untrimmed in mourning for the loss of Bologna, hands resting on the arms of his chair. Raphael's psychologically piercing portrait introduced a new informal type that would dominate papal imagery for over a century.
collection-of-beauty-pope-peter-pprubens: Saint Peter is shown in papal vestments holding the keys of heaven, his weathered features turned upward in devotion. Painted soon after Rubens's return from Italy, the half-length follows a Caravaggesque tradition of monumental, close-cropped apostle portraits.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-d-edmond-a: Seurat's friend the painter Aman-Jean is seen in profile against a darkened ground, a cigarette in hand, modeled entirely in delicate hatchings of conté crayon on textured paper. The drawing was the first work Seurat exhibited at the Salon and helped establish the velvety tonal manner of his black-and-white sheets.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-d-homme-an: A man in a feathered cap and ruff turns sharply toward the viewer, brush rapidly defining the lace and the dark eyes. Long catalogued at the Louvre as Diderot, the picture is now classed among Fragonard's figures de fantaisie, painted in roughly an hour each as virtuoso essays in costume portraiture.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-de-l-artis: Raphael places himself behind a foregrounded companion who turns to point outward, the two men linked by a cascade of hands and gazes. The double portrait is among the late, most psychologically intricate works produced in his Roman studio.

A bust-length self-portrait, the painter turned slightly with a heavy beard, set before a reversed landscape on the studio wall. Catalogued as FWN 434 and dated about 1875, the canvas was probably worked up in Armand Guillaumin's studio in Paris, whose own river view hangs behind the sitter.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-de-madame-: Henriette de Verninac, sister of Eugène Delacroix, sits half-length in an Empire dress of white muslin against an olive ground, a yellow shawl draped across her lap. Jacques-Louis David painted the portrait in 1799, exhibiting it at the Salon of that year; the Louvre acquired it in 1942 (RF 1942-16).
collection-of-beauty-portrait-de-victor-: The collector Victor Chocquet seen bust-length against patterned wallpaper, his greying hair and beard built up in close-keyed strokes. Chocquet, a customs official who amassed dozens of Impressionist canvases, was introduced to Cézanne by Renoir in 1875; the portrait dates from about 1876 to 1877.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-a-man-1: A bearded sitter in a dark coat fills the canvas at three-quarter length, hands hidden, the background washed in a flat warm grey. Dated 1877 and measuring 79 by 59 cm in oil on canvas, the portrait is in the Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, part of the deep Clark holding of Degas built up between 1911 and 1921.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-a-man-a: Half-length portrait of an ecclesiastic in dark robes, his hand resting on a closed volume. Vasari identifies the sitter as a Canon of Pisa Cathedral and close friend of the painter, credited with helping Andrea secure his final commissions before his death in 1530.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-a-monk-: A bearded religious in dark habit emerges from a shadowed ground, his lined face caught in raking light. Rubens repeatedly studied such ascetic types as preparatory heads for his larger altarpieces of saints and church fathers.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-a-woman: A bust-length likeness of a woman against a neutral ground, her face modelled with the smooth finish Boilly cultivated for small cabinet portraits. Oil on canvas, 22.2 by 17.5 cm, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Boilly produced hundreds of these compact heads for a Parisian middle-class clientele.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-alexand: The young Alexandrine Le Normant d'Etiolles holds a goldfinch on a tethered thread, daughter of Madame de Pompadour by an earlier marriage. The picture, attributed to Boucher and dated 1749, was painted during the years when the painter served as Pompadour's favourite portraitist and decorator.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-ann-for: Ann Ford sits in a fashionable Bath drawing room with her English guitar across her lap and a viola da gamba propped beside her chair. Painted in 1760 shortly after Gainsborough settled in Bath, the portrait celebrates Ford as a professional musician, a calling unusual for a woman of her class and one her father had tried to suppress.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-dr-will: Two King Charles spaniels owned by the anatomist Dr William Hunter sit alert on a stone ledge against a wooded background. Oil on canvas of around 1770, the picture is among the earliest known works by Gilbert Stuart, painted in his teens in Newport before he left for Scotland.

Two white-and-brown spotted spaniels stretch beneath a Newport Chippendale mahogany tea table, the larger asleep facing left and the smaller looking out at the viewer. Painted by the young Gilbert Stuart in Newport around 1770, the canvas is among the earliest surviving works by the future portraitist of George Washington.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-george-: The royal favorite is shown in armor with a baton of command, the Order of the Garter prominent at his knee. Long thought to be a copy, dendrochronology and technical analysis of the panel preparation now support attribution to Rubens's own studio of the 1620s.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-henri-m: The painter Henri Michel-Lévy stands in his studio leaning against his own canvases, a slack mannequin collapsed on the floorboards beside an open paintbox. Degas exhibited the 1878 portrait, now at the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon, at the fourth Impressionist exhibition under the title Artist in his Studio.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-ida-rub: The dancer Ida Rubinstein reclines nude on a strip of blue cloth, her limbs elongated into the silhouette of an Assyrian relief. Serov painted her in Paris in summer 1910 after seeing her perform Zobeide in Scheherazade and the title role in Cléopâtre for Diaghilev's first Saisons Russes. The canvas is in the State Russian Museum.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-ivan-mo: The Moscow textile heir Ivan Morozov sits in his palatial collection, the still life Fruit and Bronze by Matisse hung deliberately behind his shoulder. Valentin Serov painted the portrait in 1910, two years before his own early death; Morozov's collection of French modernism was nationalized in 1918 and forms the core of the Pushkin Museum's modern holdings.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-la-faye: A bust portrait of Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, the officer who served in the American and French revolutions. Oil on canvas, dated 1788, formerly attributed to Henri-Pierre Danloux before being given to Boilly. The sitter is shown in civilian dress against a plain ground.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-margare: Half-length portrait of the artist's wife Margaret, née Burr, the illegitimate daughter of the 3rd Duke of Beaufort. Gainsborough painted the canvas around 1778, perhaps to mark her 50th birthday, contrasting carefully observed features with rapid zigzags of paint for the black shawl. It is held by the Samuel Courtauld Trust at the Courtauld Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-mrs-the: Frances Deering Wentworth, painted at twenty in oil on canvas, holds a flying squirrel by a chain in a gesture borrowed from Copley's Pelham portrait of the same year. Married first to Theodore Atkinson Jr. and later to Governor John Wentworth, she sat to Copley in 1765 in Boston.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-peder-s: Tuxen depicts his fellow Skagen colonist Krøyer at work, palette in hand, eyes fixed on an unseen sitter. The portrait commemorates a friendship between the two leading Danish naturalist painters, set down a few years before Krøyer's mental collapse.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-princes: The young princess is presented as Iris, draped in classicizing white muslin against a stormy sky, a length of rainbow gauze trailing from her shoulder. Vigée Le Brun painted her in Vienna during the émigré years that followed the artist's flight from revolutionary France.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-sophia-: Sophia Andreevna Shuvalova, twenty years old and recently married to Count Alexei Bobrinsky, sits in a white silk gown against a backdrop of dark drapery. Bryullov, by then living in Italy on doctor's orders, completed this portrait in 1849, a few years before his death in Manziana.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-the-art: An early portrait by the teenage Vigée Le Brun shows her younger brother Étienne in elegant attire, his open expression rendered with the precocious assurance that would soon win her royal commissions. The handling already displays the porcelain finish and Rococo grace of her mature manner.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-the-wri: Maxim Gorky leans forward in a tieless dark shirt, his thin moustache and untidy hair signalling the workman writer he cultivated as a public persona. Serov painted the portrait in 1905, the year of the first Russian revolution, in which Gorky was briefly imprisoned for revolutionary agitation.
collection-of-beauty-portret-van-etienne: The Parisian restaurateur is rendered with brisk, hatched brushwork in warm browns and greens, the modeling already loosened by Van Gogh's exposure to Impressionist technique. The portrait dates from his Paris year, when he was experimenting with the divisionist touch of Seurat and Signac.
collection-of-beauty-portret-van-willem-: William II, Prince of Orange, stands in full armour with a commander's baton beside his English wife Mary Stuart on a balcony, both shown full-length. Painted in 1647 for the Stadholder's court, the double portrait belongs to the Rijksmuseum (SK-A-871) and helped fix Honthorst's reputation as the dynasty's preferred image-maker.
collection-of-beauty-pozzi-samuel-par-sa: The celebrated Parisian gynecologist Samuel Pozzi stands full length in a flame-red dressing gown, fingers tugging at his collar and sash. Sargent's bravura essay in monochrome scarlet was painted in the sitter's own apartment and announced the young American's arrival in Parisian society.
collection-of-beauty-prado-los-desastres: Plate 4 of the Disasters of War, captioned 'The women give courage'. Goya shows female combatants resisting French troops during the Peninsular War, the etching and aquatint biting through the page in his characteristically stark contrasts of black and gnawed white.

Plate 46 of the Disasters of War, 'This is bad'. A friar is set upon amid scattered bodies, the scene drawn with the cramped, shallow space and bitten line that give the series its grim moral force. The plates were withheld until decades after Goya's death.

Plate 47 of the Disasters of War, 'This is how it happened'. A clergyman is dragged and despoiled in the chaos of war, Goya pairing terse caption and unsparing image in the documentary mode that distinguishes the series from any heroic battle tradition.
collection-of-beauty-prayer-in-the-mosqu: Worshippers prostrate themselves in long rows beneath the soaring arches of Cairo's Mosque of Amr, sunlight slanting across the columns and prayer mats. Gérôme's enamel-smooth Orientalism rests on direct study of Egyptian architecture from his repeated travels in the country.
collection-of-beauty-prayers-at-sunset-u: Worshippers gather at a ghat in Udaipur as evening light falls on the lake and palace beyond. Cut and printed in 1919 by Watanabe Shozaburo's Tokyo workshop and acquired by the Honolulu Academy of Arts, the print belongs to Bartlett's Indian series produced after his 1916 tour of the subcontinent.
collection-of-beauty-print-the-flight-in: An engraving showing the Virgin and Child on the donkey under a date palm, with angels shaking down its fruit while Joseph gathers the dates. Schongauer's fine, controlled burin work and tender narrative detail set the model for later northern printmaking, including the young Dürer.
collection-of-beauty-procesion-de-pascua: A vast religious procession winds across a sunburnt steppe, sweeping clergy, peasants, gendarmes, and crippled pilgrims into a single dust-clouded cross-section of imperial Russian society. Repin's panoramic canvas is a touchstone of Peredvizhniki social realism.
collection-of-beauty-promenade-sur-la-fa: Strolling figures top a grassy clifftop above the Channel near Le Havre, with sailing vessels scattered across a breezy sea. Painted at his family's seaside resort, the picture marks Monet's emergence from Boudin's tutelage toward his own brisk plein-air idiom.
collection-of-beauty-purfleet-and-the-es: Sailing barges and Thames hoys ride the broad estuary off the chalk cliffs of Purfleet, the low Essex shore stretching beyond. The watercolor belongs to Turner's early topographical phase, when accurate maritime detail was still the foundation of his atmospheric effects.
collection-of-beauty-pythagoras-advocati: Rubens depicts the Greek philosopher gesturing toward a heap of fruit and grain as he urges his listeners to abstain from meat. The composition draws on Ovid's Metamorphoses, with abundant still-life passages painted in collaboration with Frans Snyders.
collection-of-beauty-qian-xuan-early-aut: A handscroll in ink and color on paper showing dragonflies, frogs, and aquatic plants beside a pond. Qian Xuan was a scholar-painter of the late Song and early Yuan, and the work pairs close natural observation with the lyric reserve of literati painting.
collection-of-beauty-quai-du-louvre-1867: An early Parisian cityscape, painted from a balcony of the Louvre overlooking the Seine. Bustling figures, carriages, and the dome of the Pantheon are rendered with the high vantage and bright daylight that anticipate Monet's mature Impressionist manner.
collection-of-beauty-quentin-matsys-a-gr: An ageing woman in a horned headdress and low-cut Burgundian bodice grins out of the frame, clutching a small red flower. Painted around 1513 and now in the National Gallery, London, Metsys's panel is the source for John Tenniel's Ugly Duchess in the illustrations to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
collection-of-beauty-quinten-massys-the-: Four winged angels flank a marble throne where the Virgin holds the infant Christ, painted in oil on oak with a tooled gold ground. The small panel of around 1495, in the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica in Rome, marks Metsys' transition from Leuven goldsmith to leading Antwerp painter.
collection-of-beauty-quinten-metsys-head: An elderly man in a fur-trimmed coat stares out from a near-frontal pose, the deep wrinkles around eyes and mouth recorded with quiet, forensic care. Painted around 1525, the panel reflects the late Metsys interest in physiognomic types that he pursued alongside his more grotesque caricature heads.
collection-of-beauty-rachel-strong-by-l-: Portrait of Rachel Strong, the American heiress who would marry Comte Henri de Boisgelin. Painted by Bakst in 1924 during his final months in Paris, where he had moved between theatre work for Diaghilev and society portrait commissions from wealthy expatriates.
collection-of-beauty-raffaello-madonna-c: The Virgin holds the Christ Child against a low Umbrian horizon with a church spire visible at left, the figures pyramidally composed in soft contour. Known as the Small Cowper Madonna for its nineteenth-century English owner, the panel of around 1505 is at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
collection-of-beauty-raffaello-sanzio-ri: A portrait of the young Florentine banker Bindo Altoviti, who turns over his shoulder to meet the viewer's gaze. The cool palette, soft modeling, and elegant turn of the head exemplify Raphael's late Roman portrait style.
collection-of-beauty-raimondi-lucretia-s: An engraving after a design by Raphael showing the Roman matron Lucretia about to plunge a dagger into her breast. Raimondi's burin work helped establish reproductive printmaking as a vehicle for disseminating Italian Renaissance invention across Europe.
