Despite the title, Les Liliacees covers many Iridaceae beyond true lilies, as the Jussieu line on the plate shows.
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-ringens: Gladiolus ringens is set apart by its violet-scented flowers, yellow and reddish, borne in a loose arched spike with sheathing leaves longer than the stem. The two-lipped funnel-shaped corolla is shown open. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-strictiflorus: Gladiolus strictiflorus, with spirally twisted lance-shaped leaves in two opposite ranks and a fairly loose spike of dark flowers around the scape. The botanist A.P. de Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text printed beside Redoute's plates. From the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-strictus: Gladiolus strictus, long confused with the plaited gladiolus, its whole surface covered in soft bristling hairs and its pleated leaves topped by a spike of blue-lilac flowers. The bottle-shaped bulb is shown below. This plate is from the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-tristis: Gladiolus tristis is recognised at once by its rush-like leaves grooved with three or four longitudinal furrows, the stem bearing usually two pale-yellow flowers tinged brown outside. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand. From the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-tubatus: Gladiolus tubatus, close to the leaning gladiolus, with hairy pleated leaves and a scape that bends horizontal to carry twelve or fourteen long-tubed flowers in a loose spike. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809); enlarged floral figures sit at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-tubiflorus: Gladiolus tubiflorus grows from an ovoid brown bulb, its sword-shaped pleated leaves clasping the hairy scape, which divides into four or five branches of crowded two-ranked flowers. The hairy three-valved spathe is shown enlarged below. From the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-undulatus: Gladiolus undulatus, from a white irregular tuber, carries four or five erect scentless flowers with wavy, half-reflexed segments and a slender purple-red tube. The lower segments are streaked purple in one variety. This plate appears in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-watsonius: Gladiolus watsonius rises on a slender, arched stem with stiff, glaucous leaves grooved on each face, carrying two scarlet flowers veined in yellow and spotted within. The plate belongs to the iris family in Jussieu's arrangement; Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-gladiolus-xanthospilus: Gladiolus xanthospilus, a flexed stem of five or six knife-shaped leaves topped by white flowers scattered with sulphur-yellow blotches. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), the stipple engraving printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-globba-erecta: Globba erecta sends up erect herbaceous stems with lanceolate leaves and a terminal raceme of small flowers mottled white, yellow and red. The plate places it among the Balisiers (canna family) in Jussieu's order; the enlarged floral parts below follow the botanical convention of the day.
redoute-lilies-globba-nutans: Globba nutans, a tall reed-like stem with long oblong leaves and a nodding raceme that lifts as the buds, rose-and-white and varnished in sheen, open. It appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), the stipple engraving coloured from a single plate and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-haemanthus-albiflos: Haemanthus albiflos, a thick bristly scape carrying a dense umbel of white flowers enclosed in a spathe of green-veined bracts, with orange anthers on long projecting filaments. A red berry and seed figure sit at the foot; Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-haemanthus-coccineus: Haemanthus coccineus, two broad tongue-shaped leaves spread on the ground beside a spotted scape opening into a scarlet involucre that holds a tight umbel of red flowers. The name means blood-flower; the plate appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-haemanthus-multiflorus: Haemanthus multiflorus, a spotted scape bearing a globe-like umbel of bright red flowers with long projecting filaments, set beside an erect tuft of ribbed leaves. The plate belongs to the Narcisses family in Jussieu's order; Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-haemanthus-puniceus: Haemanthus puniceus, a tuft of wavy ovate leaves spotted with purple beside a thick scape ending in a dense umbel of pale-red flowers within a green spathe. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across the eight folio volumes.
redoute-lilies-hedychium-coronarium: Hedychium coronarium, a tall leafy stem with distichous oblong leaves and a terminal spike whose flowers carry a broad heart-notched lip. The plate places it among the Balisiers in Jussieu's order; Redoute drew it for the eighth and last volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-heliconia-humilis: Heliconia humilis, its banana-like sheathing petioles forming the stem and supporting broad lanceolate leaves, with a spike of boat-shaped spathes set in two opposite ranks. The plate belongs to the Bananiers family in Jussieu's order, drawn for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-heliconia-psittacorum: Heliconia psittacorum, a smooth banana-like stem ending in an erect spike with an orange bract tipped in black, the seven or eight orange flowers marked with black and clear yellow. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), printed in colour and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-helonias-bullata: Helonias bullata, a hollow stem rising above orchid-like basal leaves to a dense oblong spike of small, fragrant pink flowers on short pedicels. The plate places it among the rushes (Joncs) in Jussieu's order; it appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-hemerocallis-caerulea: Hemerocallis caerulea, broad stalked leaves and a bare scape ending in a raceme of bell-shaped flowers in pale blue tinged with lilac, the tube grooved with six furrows. The dissection figures show the enlarged stamens and style, a botanical convention of Redoute's day.
redoute-lilies-hemerocallis-flava: Hemerocallis flava, the common yellow daylily, with keeled linear leaves and a branched scape bearing fragrant funnel-shaped flowers in a loose corymb. Its straight, non-anastomosing veins distinguish it from the tawny species; the plate appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-hemerocallis-fulva: Hemerocallis fulva, the tawny daylily, larger in every part than the yellow species, its broad keeled leaves and funnel-shaped flowers in a loose corymb running fawn to reddish. The plate appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), the stipple engraving printed in colour and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-hemerocallis-japonica: Hemerocallis japonica, set apart by its broad heart-shaped leaves narrowed to channelled petioles and a loose spike of large white bell-shaped flowers on thick pale pedicels. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-heritiera-tinctorum: Heritiera tinctorum, a leafy stem with sword-shaped basal leaves and a tight corymb of woolly-coated flowers, orange within and split into six segments. The plate places it among the iris family in Jussieu's order; Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-hyacinthus-amethystinus: Hyacinthus amethystinus, a small bulb sending up linear channelled leaves and a slender scape with five or six tubular blue flowers on short pedicels. The plate belongs to the Asphodeles in Jussieu's order; it appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-hyacinthus-orientalis: Hyacinthus orientalis, the garden hyacinth, its bulb sending up strap-shaped leaves and a hampe with a loose raceme of funnel-form flowers, the segments reflexed and ribbed. Redoute drew it for the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814), printed in colour and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-hyacinthus-romanus: Hyacinthus romanus, slender scapes rising above keeled linear leaves to a loose cylindrical raceme of about twenty small flowers that pass from greenish to white. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine; this plate ran in the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-hyacinthus-serotinus: Hyacinthus serotinus, an ash-red scape carrying a one-sided raceme of dingy greenish-yellow flowers, the bell-shaped perigone in two ranks of lobes. A three-celled capsule figure sits below; the plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-hyacinthus-viridis: Hyacinthus viridis, a slender scape with a loose raceme of six or seven green flowers whose outer segments taper almost to threads, set above narrow linear leaves. The plate belongs to the Asphodeles in Jussieu's order, drawn for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-hypoxis-erecta: Hypoxis erecta, hairy linear leaves in a tuft above a brown-tunicked base, with two-edged scapes bearing four or five small yellow flowers green on their undersides. The plate places it among the Narcisses in Jussieu's order; Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-hypoxis-luzulaefolia: Hypoxis luzulaefolia, pleated linear leaves edged with hooked cilia and a hairy scape ending in a single greenish-yellow flower split to the base into six segments. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809), the stipple engraving printed in colour and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-hypoxis-sobolifera: Hypoxis sobolifera, its hairy linear-lanceolate leaves rising from a thick knotted rootstock to scapes bearing two to four yellow six-parted flowers. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), where Jussieu placed it among the Narcissus family.
redoute-lilies-hypoxis-stellata: Hypoxis stellata, a single bright yellow star-shaped flower on a stiff scape, each segment marked with a brown spot at its base, above narrow leaves spread along the ground. The plate is a stipple engraving printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across all eight folio volumes.
redoute-lilies-iris-amoena: Iris amoena, its upright leaves reddish at the base and nearly as long as the stem, with bearded outer segments that curve back only at the tip. Redoute treated it as a new species, possibly the same as the Hungarian iris, in the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-iris-arenaria: Iris arenaria, one of the smallest species of its genus, with sword-shaped leaves and pale yellow flowers borne in pairs on short stems. The outer segments are bearded past the middle, the inner ones upright and wavy below; A.P. de Candolle supplied the accompanying botanical text.
redoute-lilies-iris-cristata: Iris cristata, a small species with creeping leafy runners and a triple crest along the outer perigon segments, each bearing a yellow blotch ringed in violet. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812); the dissection figures enlarge the flower's parts in the convention of the day.
redoute-lilies-iris-curtopetala: Iris curtopetala, its sword-shaped pale green leaves overtopping the flattened stem, with three yellow flowers veined in violet and ridged near the base of the outer segments. The stipple plate was printed in colour from a single engraving and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-iris-fimbriata: Iris fimbriata, distinguished by the fringed and shredded tips of its stigma segments, its pale blue flowers washed with white and spotted yellow on the larger lobes. Jussieu placed it among the Iridaceae; Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-iris-flavescens: Iris flavescens, with sword-shaped pleated leaves and three or four yellowish-white flowers grouped at each branch tip, the outer segments bearded and veined in violet-purple at the base. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-iris-florentina: Iris florentina, the white-flowered Florentine iris, its glaucous sword-shaped leaves shorter than the scape and its root strongly scented when dried. The accompanying text distinguishes it from the violet German iris, which it closely resembles in form and size.
redoute-lilies-iris-foetidissima: Iris foetidissima, whose leaves give off a roasted-meat odour when crushed, bearing small dull blue-violet flowers two to a stem. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811); the foliage is often striped lengthwise in alternating green and yellow.
redoute-lilies-iris-germanica: Iris germanica, its fleshy knotted rootstock sending up glaucous falcate leaves and a branched stem of violet to pale blue flowers. The outer segments are bearded with dense yellow filaments along the midline; A.P. de Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text.
redoute-lilies-iris-graminea: Iris graminea, recognised by stems much shorter than its bright green grass-like leaves, with two or three flowers veined blue on a whitish ground. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809), where Jussieu placed it among the Iris family.
redoute-lilies-iris-lurida: Iris lurida, its cylindrical creeping rootstock giving rise to upright leaves and flowers whose limb is a glossy blackish-purple, the outer segments bearded in yellow and lined with yellow and violet at the base. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-iris-lutescens: Iris lutescens, a low species bearing a single yellow terminal flower above sword-shaped leaves, the outer spatulate segments deeper in colour and bearded with yellow filaments. The plate is a stipple engraving printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-iris-martinicensis: Iris martinicensis, a solid tuber sending up a bare stem topped by a cluster of bright yellow flowers spotted with black, the segments opening in succession. The enlarged figures at the foot of the sheet show the three stamens and the short style with its yellow stigmas.
redoute-lilies-iris-monnieri: Iris monnieri, a tall species reaching one or two metres, its sword-shaped leaves sheathing the stem below three or four large yellow flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the inner segments run longer than the stigmas, setting it apart from the yellow flag.
redoute-lilies-iris-ochroleuca: Iris ochroleuca, reaching nearly a metre, its outer segments tipped with a large whitish elliptical blade above a yellow claw, the inner segments and stigmas white. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811), distinguishing it from a closely allied species.
redoute-lilies-iris-pallida: Iris pallida, a tall species rising to a metre or more from a knotted rootstock, with glaucous falcate leaves and large pale blue scented flowers. The outer segments are bearded with white-and-yellow filaments and shade to lilac-violet; Redoute drew it for the seventh volume (1812).
redoute-lilies-iris-persica: Iris persica, the Persian iris, shown in flower with its narrow leaves in a plate from Redoute's Les Liliacees. The work was issued in eight folio volumes between 1802 and 1816, its plates printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-iris-plicata: Iris plicata, rising to a metre with glaucous sword-shaped leaves and strongly scented flowers, the outer segments whitish at the centre and violet at the wavy edges, veined purple at the base. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-iris-pratensis: Iris pratensis, its very narrow sword-shaped leaves and hollow stem bearing three or four scented blue flowers, the outer segments spatulate with a yellow claw veined in violet. Many specimens Redoute painted were grown in the gardens at Malmaison, where he served Empress Josephine.
redoute-lilies-iris-pseudacorus: Iris pseudacorus, the common yellow flag of Europe, with entirely yellow beardless flowers whose inner segments fall short of the stigmas. Its sheathing sword-shaped leaves shorten upward into bracts; Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-iris-pumila: Iris pumila, the dwarf iris, shown in flower above its short sword-shaped leaves in a plate from Redoute's Les Liliacees. The image is a stipple engraving printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-iris-sambucina: Iris sambucina, named for its elder-scented flowers, two to each branch above falcate sword-shaped leaves marked with raised veins. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811), where Jussieu placed it among the Iris family.
redoute-lilies-iris-scorpioides: Plate 211 shows Iris scorpioides, its glossy channelled leaves rising around three successive blue flowers with a long slender perigone tube and very small inner lobes. From the Iridaceae as classified on the sheet (Triandria monogynia in the Linnaean system); the stipple engraving was printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-iris-sibirica-b: Iris sibirica on a tall hollow stem, its narrow sword-shaped leaves nearly as long as the stalk and two or three pedicelled flowers with white-margined outer segments and erect inner ones. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814), the descriptive text supplied by Candolle and his colleagues.
redoute-lilies-iris-sibirica-c: A slender small-flowered form of Iris sibirica, its thin scape carrying two flowers from a terminal spathe above narrow bright-green leaves; the falls are pale lilac, yellow at the base with violet veins. Candolle treated it as a variety of the Siberian iris though possibly a distinct species. Plate 420, Les Liliacees, 1812.
redoute-lilies-iris-sisyrinchium-29: Plate 29 shows Iris sisyrinchium, named for its unusual root of two solid bulbs set one above the other, with a cylindrical stem and two or three flowers opening in succession. The French text notes it grows wild across southern Europe; Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees in 1802.
redoute-lilies-iris-sisyrinchium-458: A pale-violet form of Iris sisyrinchium on a wiry rush-like stem barely a decimetre high, the lilac falls marked near the claw with a white and yellowish patch and the inner segments lanceolate. The plate belongs to the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814); enlarged figures of the flower parts sit at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-iris-spuria: Plate 349 shows Iris spuria, its sword-shaped glaucous leaves below a tall stem bearing three or four flowers with spatulate, widely spread outer segments; the claw is yellow with red veins and the blade deep violet. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and watercoloured by hand.
redoute-lilies-iris-squalens: Iris squalens on a branching stem, its outer falls purple toward the tip and yellowish at the base with purple veins, the midline bearded with yellow filaments tipped purple. Candolle records that some botanists treated it as a mere variety of the elder-scented iris. Plate 365, Les Liliacees, 1812.
redoute-lilies-iris-stenogyna: Plate 310 shows Iris stenogyna, named for its narrow stigmas, with sword-shaped glaucous leaves and two scentless yellowish flowers emerging from a three-valved spathe. The ribbed oblong ovary and greenish-yellow segments are drawn from life; Redoute made the plate for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees in 1811.
redoute-lilies-iris-suziana: Plate 18 shows Iris suziana, distinguished by its single very large flower mottled white and blackish-purple, the falls reflexed and bearded with violet hairs at the base. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, and many specimens for the work came from the gardens at Malmaison. From the first volume of Les Liliacees, 1802.
redoute-lilies-iris-swertii: Iris swertii on a glaucous stem about three decimetres high, usually carrying three flowers whose outer segments are white-bearded along the midline and the inner ones spatulate and waved. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used throughout the eight folio volumes.
redoute-lilies-iris-triflora: Plate 481 shows Iris triflora, forming dense low tufts of bright green, its leaf-sheaths each enclosing about three blue white-veined flowers that open one after another. The descriptive text for Les Liliacees was supplied by Candolle and others; this plate appeared in the eighth volume, 1814.
redoute-lilies-iris-tuberosa: Plate 48 shows Iris tuberosa, named for a root of two or three thick cylindrical tubers, with four-angled grooved leaves and a single dull-green flower whose outer segments are tipped deep purple. Tournefort once made it the type of a separate genus; Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees in 1802.
redoute-lilies-iris-variegata: Plate 292 shows Iris variegata, its sword-shaped leaves below a branched stem with two or three flowers; the outer segments are yellow streaked with red-violet and bearded along the midline, the inner ones wholly yellow. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and watercoloured by hand.
redoute-lilies-iris-versicolor: Iris versicolor on a slender scape, its small flowers with lance-shaped falls ending in a rounded purple-violet blade that turns strongly outward, the rest dull yellow veined with violet. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811), part of a work spanning 1802 to 1816.
redoute-lilies-iris-virescens: Plate 295 shows Iris virescens, its sword-shaped leaves below a short stem bearing one yellowish flower in a two-valved spathe; the outer segments are lilac above and yellow with violet veins below, bearded with yellow filaments. From the fifth volume of Les Liliacees, 1809.
redoute-lilies-iris-xiphium: Plate 337 shows Iris xiphium, the most variable of its genus in flower size and colour, growing from a white ovoid tuber rather than a true bulb, with awl-shaped channelled leaves and usually two terminal flowers. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-iris-xyphioides: Plate 212 shows Iris xyphioides, an ovoid bulb sending up a stem to four or six decimetres with two large blue flowers tinged violet, some specimens speckled with darker spots. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine; this plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees, 1807.
redoute-lilies-ixia-anemonaeflora: Plate 85 shows Ixia anemonaeflora from a whitish ovoid bulb, its slender stem leafy nearly to the top and carrying two or three spaced white flowers tinged yellow at the throat. Despite the title, Les Liliacees covers many monocot families; this Ixia belongs to the Iridaceae, as the classification line records.
redoute-lilies-ixia-bulbifera: Ixia bulbifera, distinguished by its torn scarious bracts, pale funnel-shaped flowers and small bulbs in the leaf axils of an often-branched stem. The blooms range from yellowish white to citron yellow, sometimes spotted purple at the base. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees, 1805.
redoute-lilies-ixia-bulbocodium: Plate 88 shows Ixia bulbocodium, set apart by a simple scape shorter than the leaves and bearing a single flower, with a stigma so deeply split it appears six-parted. The text notes wide variation, the small-flowered race shown here under a decimetre tall with white, bluish or violet blooms.
redoute-lilies-ixia-candida: Ixia candida grows from a flattened orbicular bulb, its few sword-shaped leaves sheathing the lower stem below a sparse pyramidal raceme of ten or twelve flowers between whitish scarious bracts. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand; from the eighth volume of Les Liliacees, 1814.
redoute-lilies-ixia-cepacea: Plate 96 shows Ixia cepacea, named for hollow cylindrical leaves like an onion's, with a simple stem ending in a flat two-ranked spike of pale grey-blue flowers. Each funnel-shaped bloom sits between two opposite membranous bracts; Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees in 1804.
redoute-lilies-ixia-conica: Plate 138 shows Ixia conica, its orange flowers marked with black spots at the base of the segments and gathered into a dense rounded spike, the corolla conical before opening. The style divides into three stigmas only near the anther tips. From the third volume of Les Liliacees, 1805.
redoute-lilies-ixia-crispa: Ixia crispa on a hand-high flexuous stem with three or four alternate flowers, its narrow awl-shaped leaves crisped and symmetrically frilled either side of a transparent midrib, the tips twisting into a tendril. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814), the botanical text supplied by Candolle and others.
redoute-lilies-ixia-crocata: Ixia crocata rises on a slender stem to a loose spike of orange-yellow funnel-shaped flowers, its sword-shaped leaves curved like a sickle below. The classification line places it in the iris family, Triandria monogynia of the Linnaean system. Enlarged stamen and ovary figures sit at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-ixia-dubia: Ixia dubia carries a dense, nearly globular spike of golden-yellow saucer-shaped flowers, each segment marked with a purple blotch at its base. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1804. The slim leaves are folded sword-fashion along the lower stem.
redoute-lilies-ixia-filifolia: Ixia filifolia bears solitary terminal flowers, sometimes bright yellow and sometimes reddish, above very fine thread-like leaves. The French text notes its close kinship with Ixia rosea, from which it differs by its shorter foliage. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-ixia-filiformis: Ixia filiformis shows a dense crimson spike at the top of a fine, slender scape twice the length of its sword-shaped leaves. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802). The flowers turn mostly to one side in a nodding, tightly packed head.
redoute-lilies-ixia-fusco-citrina: Ixia fusco-citrina carries a short head of jonquil-yellow flowers, each division stained with a brown lustrous blotch at its inner base. The plate belongs to the iris family in the Linnaean class Triandria monogynia. Below, the dissection figures enlarge the flower's stamens in the period's botanical convention.
redoute-lilies-ixia-grandiflora-139: Ixia grandiflora bears large, erect, violet-purple flowers from membranous spathes torn into narrow reflexed strips. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees, published in 1805. A white spot marks the base of each funnel-shaped lobe.
redoute-lilies-ixia-grandiflora-362: Ixia grandiflora, the large-flowered corn lily of the iris family, set on its slender flowering stem. This plate appeared in the seventh volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1812. The plates were stipple engravings printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-ixia-hyalina: Ixia hyalina shows a fairly dense spike of large crimson-pink flowers, the lobes transparent along their lower margins. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, and many of the specimens he drew were grown at Malmaison. The sword-shaped leaves run shorter at the base of the stem.
redoute-lilies-ixia-liliago: Ixia liliago carries two or three large flowers resembling those of the white lily, whitish outside and yellowish within, with a dark violet spot at the inner base of each segment. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804). Enlarged stamen figures sit at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-ixia-longiflora: Ixia longiflora bears oblong segments spread above a slender cylindrical tube the length of a finger, set in a loose spike along the stem. The French text notes several varieties, one white flushed with rose and banded yellow on the lower divisions. The work belongs to the iris family in Triandria monogynia.
redoute-lilies-ixia-maculata: Ixia maculata shows a tightly packed, nearly head-like spike of star-spread flowers, each division darker at its base than above. The text notes its countless garden varieties, a collection of which Jacquin gathered at Schonbrunn. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees in 1805.
redoute-lilies-ixia-miniata: Ixia miniata carries its flowers in alternating two-ranked spikes, the corolla lobes opaque at their lower margins rather than transparent. The classification line places it in the iris family, Triandria monogynia. The glaucous-green leaves are folded sword-fashion along the lower stem.
redoute-lilies-ixia-patens: Ixia patens shows a dense terminal spike of carmine-red flowers, the bell-shaped limb divided into six oblong segments white at the base. Long grown by Dutch gardeners, it was known by the common name Ixia Kermes. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-ixia-phlogiflora: Ixia phlogiflora bears phlox-like flowers in two ranks along a slightly zigzag axis, all turning to one side as they open. The sword-shaped leaves curve like a sickle, with cartilaginous translucent veins. The descriptive text accompanying Redoute's plates was supplied by botanists of the day.
redoute-lilies-ixia-plantaginea: Ixia plantaginea carries many small deep-blue flowers, two-ranked and packed into a flattened imbricated spike, above sword-shaped leaves curved like a scythe. The plate places it in the iris family, here under the Linnaean class Hexandria monogynia. The flattened stem is two-edged.
redoute-lilies-ixia-polystachia: Ixia polystachia bears a branched spike of bell-shaped flowers, white in one variety and red-striped in another, the three outer segments slightly longer. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees in 1805. Enlarged stamen and pistil figures sit at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-ixia-radiata: Ixia radiata shows a one-sided terminal spike, the outer segments veined with purple and reflexed when the flower is fully open, the inner three concave and white. The plate comes from the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1814. A dissection of the ovary and three stigmas sits below.
redoute-lilies-ixia-rapunculoides: Ixia rapunculoides carries ten or eleven lilac bell-shaped flowers in a pyramidal raceme atop a slender, half-transparent scape. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814). The branches curve upward at their base, then run almost horizontal.
redoute-lilies-ixia-recurva: Ixia recurva bears solitary greenish-yellow flowers above sharply arched basal leaves, on a triangular stem winged with a fine brown membrane. The French text assigns it to the section Gawler set apart as Trichonema, marked by hairy filaments. The plate belongs to the iris family in Triandria monogynia.
redoute-lilies-ixia-scillaris: Ixia scillaris shows small rose-coloured flowers in loose elongated spikes along the stem and branches, resembling those of a squill. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, and many of these specimens were grown at Malmaison. The iris-like leaves are folded along their inner edge.
redoute-lilies-ixia-secunda: Ixia secunda gathers about eight flowers into a one-sided spike, the three outer violet-blue segments entire and the inner three paler and notched. The slender flexuous scape is covered in very short hairs that make it appear downy. The plate comes from the seventh volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1812.
redoute-lilies-ixia-tricolor: Ixia tricolor carries three or four large flowers in a loose spike, each lobe citron-yellow at the base, brown-purple at the middle, and bright vermilion-red at the tip. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805). Below, the enlarged anthers shed a yellow pollen in the dissection figures.
redoute-lilies-ixia-viridiflora: Ixia viridiflora bears its green flowers in a long terminal spike, two-ranked and sessile in the axils of translucent spathes streaked with rust. The leaves are linear and sword-shaped with five pale veins. The plate comes from the eighth volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1814.
redoute-lilies-kaempferia-angustifolia: Kaempferia angustifolia rises from a cluster of fleshy spindle-shaped tubers to two or three ovate-lanceolate leaves, the flowers borne between their bases. The French text credits its introduction to Willdenow, from the Berlin garden catalogue. The plate places it in the ginger family, Monandria monogynia of the Linnaean system.
redoute-lilies-koempferia-galanga: Kaempferia galanga, its broad ovate leaves spread flat and its white six-parted flower rising from bracts at the rootstock, with one inner segment deeply cleft. The aromatic rhizome places it in the Zingiberaceae; Redoute drew the plate for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-koempferia-longa: Kaempferia longa, whose flower pushes from the ground in a distinct spathe before or with the rolled, oblong leaves marked by a reddish central blotch. De Candolle's text noted specimens observed at Malmaison and in the garden of Cels. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-lachenalia-angustifolia: Lachenalia angustifolia, the smallest of its genus, with long narrow half-cylindrical leaves and a raceme of bell-shaped flowers, dull white tipped green, on a purple-flecked stalk. Enlarged stamen and ovary figures sit at the foot of the sheet, following the botanical convention of the day.
redoute-lilies-lachenalia-lanceaefolia: Lachenalia lanceaefolia, set apart by an outsized whitish bulb and a rosette of thick ovate-lanceolate leaves, the young foliage spotted green. Its small flowers crowd two flexed flowering stalks, half-pendent and reddening as they open. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-lachenalia-luteola: Lachenalia luteola, with two linear leaves free of the dark spots of its kin and a smooth stalk carrying about fifteen pendent yellow flowers, topped by small sterile pink blooms. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809), printed in colour from one plate and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-lachenalia-pallida: Lachenalia pallida, named for its pale flowers, with two long narrow channelled leaves and a short raceme on a stalk sometimes dotted red. The bell-shaped flowers carry six petals in two ranks, the upper sterile ones forming a tuft of purple bracts. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-lachenalia-pendula: Lachenalia pendula, its cylindrical poppy-red flowers tipped brown and over four centimetres long, hanging in a loose raceme that stands erect before flowering and droops at pollination. The species belongs to the Asphodel family in the Jussieu classification printed on the sheet.
redoute-lilies-lachenalia-tricolor: Lachenalia tricolor, easily known by the brown spots flecking its leaves and stalk, bearing a loose raceme of pendent flowers with orange outer segments and longer yellow inner ones on orange pedicels. Redoute drew it as plate 2 of the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-leucoium-aestivum: Leucoium aestivum, the summer snowflake, its umbel of four to six nodding white bells hung from triangular pedicels above a winged hollow stalk, each segment tipped with a green callus. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); stamen and ovary figures appear below.
redoute-lilies-leucoium-autumnale: Leucoium autumnale, the autumn snowflake, its slender threadlike leaves and one or two small white nodding bells on a fine stalk. The plate belongs to the Narcissus family in the Jussieu classification line and was drawn for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-leucoium-grandiflorum: Leucoium grandiflorum, growing from a cherry-sized bulb with narrow grassy leaves and a slender stalk bearing two white nodding flowers, each segment veined and bell-arranged. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); de Candolle's text records that the fruit was never seen.
redoute-lilies-leucoium-trichophyllum: Leucoium trichophyllum, with three or four very fine linear leaves and a slender stalk carrying one or two small flowers, white in one variety and rose in another. The pointed segments lack the apical callus of related snowflakes. The plate was drawn for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-lilium-bulbiferum: Lilium bulbiferum, the orange or fire lily, named for the small dark bulbils that form in its leaf axils. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), one of the true lilies among the many monocot families the work covers. It was printed in colour from a single plate and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-lilium-canadense: Lilium canadense, the Canada lily, with whorled lance-shaped leaves and nodding bell-formed flowers on long pedicels. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811); he served as flower painter to Empress Josephine, in whose Malmaison gardens many specimens were grown.
redoute-lilies-lilium-candidum: Lilium candidum, the Madonna lily, with its erect stem, lance-shaped leaves and trumpet-formed white flowers. The plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), a stipple engraving printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand in watercolour, the method used throughout the eight folio volumes.
redoute-lilies-lilium-chalcedonicum: Lilium chalcedonicum, the scarlet Turk's-cap lily, with whorled leaves and pendent flowers whose segments roll fully back. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809); the descriptive text accompanying Redoute's plates was supplied by A.P. de Candolle and others.
redoute-lilies-lilium-martagon: Lilium martagon, the Turk's-cap lily, known among the reflexed-petalled whorled-leaf lilies by its broad ovate-lanceolate leaves with five veins. Its orange-red flowers are spotted dark inside, with white-flowered and double forms in cultivation. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-lilium-penduliflorum: Lilium penduliflorum, rising to five or six decimetres with whorled three-veined leaves and a single nodding orange flower spotted brown within. Its six funnel-formed petals end in fleshy callused points. Stamen and pistil figures sit below, following the botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-lilium-philadelphicum: Lilium philadelphicum, the wood lily, with whorled ovate-oblong leaves and a single erect orange-red flower, yellow within at the base and spotted dark toward the clawed petals. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804), one of the North American lilies in the work.
redoute-lilies-lilium-pomponium: Lilium pomponium, its scarlet flowers in a terminal cluster, nodding earthward with petals coiled fully back, above a leafy stalk whose lower leaves are whorled. Redoute drew it as plate 7 of the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), a stipple engraving printed in colour and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-lilium-pumilum: Lilium pumilum, a miniature of the pompon and Chalcedonian lilies but with glabrous leaves, growing barely two decimetres from a white scaly bulb. Its single pendent scarlet flower has six lanceolate segments rolled back. The plate belongs to the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-lilium-superbum: Lilium superbum, the swamp lily, tall with three-veined lance-shaped leaves whorled below and numerous nodding orange-yellow flowers spotted dark, the petals reflexed as in the martagon. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804); the club-shaped seed capsule appears alongside.
redoute-lilies-lilium-tigrinum: Lilium tigrinum, the tiger lily, its tall woolly stem bearing scattered linear-lanceolate leaves with small black bulbils in their axils. The red-orange flowers are spotted purple inside and reflexed. The plate belongs to the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812); this young plant carried a single flower.
redoute-lilies-lilium-tigrinum-475: Lilium tigrinum drawn again in maturity, taller and many-flowered, its stem producing pea-sized purple-brown bulbils in the leaf axils that root readily. De Candolle's text traces it to the gardens of China and Japan. This second plate appeared in the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-lilum-pyrenaicum: Lilium pyrenaicum, the Pyrenean lily, its firm stem hung with one to three nodding yellow flowers whose six recurved petals carry dark inner spotting above narrow lance-shaped leaves. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the cultivated form bears more blooms than the wild plant.
redoute-lilies-limodorum-purpureum: Limodorum purpureum, an orchid rising from a whitish tuber to a loose raceme of purple-red flowers, each corolla split into six deep segments on two ranks. Despite the work's title, Les Liliacees ranges across many monocot families, including the orchids shown here.
redoute-lilies-limodorum-tankerwillae: Limodorum tankerwillae, an orchid whose large parts let de Candolle's text examine the family's structure in detail, with five or six veratrum-like leaves and a tall raceme of two to thirteen flowers. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-maranta-arundinacea: Maranta arundinacea, the arrowroot, with reed-like jointed stems, ovate-pointed leaves sheathing at the base, and single white flowers borne on short forked pedicels. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-massonia-angustifolia: Massonia angustifolia, a Cape bulb bearing two fleshy leaves and a stemless cluster of flowers half-hidden between their bases, each with a whitish tube and six narrow recurved lobes. The botanist de Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plates.
redoute-lilies-massonia-pustulata: Massonia pustulata, a low Cape bulb of the asphodel group, set with its paired ground-hugging leaves and tufted cluster of flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), the plate printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-massonia-violacea: Massonia violacea, a small bulb with two opposed basal leaves and a short central scape carrying slender pedicels of lilac-violet flowers, each a funnel of six recurved lobes. The plate dissection figures at the foot of the sheet enlarge the stamens and seed, a botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-mayanthemum-bifolium: Maianthemum bifolium, the two-leaved May lily, shown with its heart-based leaves and small white flowers. Redoute placed it in the asparagus family on the Jussieu classification line; the plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-mayanthemum-canadense: Maianthemum canadense, the Canada May lily, distinguished from its European cousin by near-sessile, more oblong leaves, glabrous on both faces, with sharper reticulated veining. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-medeola-angustifolia: Medeola angustifolia, a slender climbing vine to about two metres, its scattered narrow leaves and small terminal clusters of six-parted flowers, the outer segments greenish and the inner whitish. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-medeola-asparagoides: Medeola asparagoides, a twining climber of one to one and a half metres with short two-ranked branches, glossy bright-green ovate leaves, and pendent bell-shaped flowers of six greenish-white segments. Many specimens drawn for the work were grown in Empress Josephine's gardens at Malmaison.
redoute-lilies-melanthium-gramineum: Melanthium gramineum, the grass-leaved species, growing from a scaly bulb that buds offsets, with narrow basal leaves and two or three sessile whitish flowers tinged yellow. The corolla divides to the base into six lance-linear segments marked with even longitudinal veins.
redoute-lilies-merendera-bulbocodium: Merendera bulbocodium, long confused with the spring meadow saffron it resembles, distinguished by its three basally united ovaries each topped by a separate style. Per the supplied text it carries the corolla of Bulbocodium, the pistil of Colchicum, and the anther of saffron.
redoute-lilies-methonica-superba: Methonica superba, the glory lily, its leaves tipped with curling tendrils and flame-coloured flowers whose wavy petals rise back with the base yellow marked red. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802); the slender stem reaches some two metres.
redoute-lilies-montbretia-securigera: Montbretia securigera, an iris-family plant from two small white bulbs, its sword-shaped basal leaves and a simple spike of three to five orange-yellow funnel flowers, the lower lobes bearing a pale auricle within a reddish blotch. The plate appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-moraea-sordescens: Moraea sordescens, a low iris-family plant under three decimetres, with spathes of two flowers some three to four centimetres across, dull reddish and marked by three red-edged yellow blotches. De Candolle worked from an unpublished L'Heritier drawing in describing it.
redoute-lilies-moroea-iridioides: Moraea iridioides, near to the irises for its large petal-like stigmas, its fan of flat sword-shaped leaves and stalked flowers mingling white, yellow, and blue. It sits among the Moraeas because the six corolla segments spread nearly equal, the outer trio yellow-spotted at the base.
redoute-lilies-moroea-vaginata: Moraea vaginata, an iris-family plant whose flower stalk stays sheathed for its whole length inside an upper leaf, so the blooms seem to spring from the side of a flattened stem. Its fan of compressed dark-green basal leaves reaches six or seven decimetres.
redoute-lilies-musa-coccinea: Musa coccinea, the scarlet banana, smaller than the long-known banana species but like them in form, with sheathing leaf-stalks and a dense erect spike wrapped in large coloured spathes. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-musa-paradisiaca: Musa paradisiaca, the cultivated banana, its herbaceous trunk of sheathed leaf-stalks rising four to five metres to a crown of six or seven huge leaves up to two metres long. Redoute drew it for the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-muscari-ambrosiacum: Muscari ambrosiacum, the musk grape hyacinth that named the genus, its ovoid white bulb sending up a dense raceme of small urn-shaped flowers in a dull greyish-yellow that turns russet after fertilisation. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-muscari-botryoides: Muscari botryoides, with firm linear channelled leaves and one or two scapes bearing a near-cylindrical raceme of almost spherical bright-blue flowers, each rimmed by six small white recurved teeth. The plate dissection figures below enlarge the black heart-shaped anthers and ovary.
redoute-lilies-muscari-comosum: Muscari comosum, the tassel grape hyacinth, drawn with its raceme topped by a tuft of sterile coloured flowers. Redoute placed it among the asphodels; the plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-muscari-racemosum: Muscari racemosum, growing from an ovoid bulb with several offsets, its slender drooping linear leaves and erect scape carrying a short, tight raceme of deep blue-violet flowers. The whole plant is glabrous, the small bracts borne on roughly horizontal pedicels.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-biflorus: Narcissus biflorus, the two-flowered daffodil, its scape carrying a pair of whitish blooms above narrow grey-green leaves, with the enlarged stamen and seed figures at the foot of the sheet. Long confused with the poet's narcissus until Curtis fixed its distinguishing characters; Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-bulbocodium: Narcissus bulbocodium, the hoop-petticoat daffodil, a single yellow flower whose funnel-shaped nectary runs longer than the six narrow corolla segments, set above slender linear leaves. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method Redoute used across the eight folio volumes of Les Liliacees.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-calathinus-a: Narcissus calathinus, the large-cup daffodil, a rounded bulb giving two flat linear leaves and a tall scape ending in two large yellow flowers, each with a broad petaloid cup as long as the spreading perianth lobes. From the family of Narcisses in Jussieu's classification; Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-calathinus-b: A variety of Narcissus calathinus, two nodding flowers on unequal stalks above narrow dark-green leaves, the white perianth segments faintly tinged yellow and turned up around a bell-shaped crown. De Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plates; this one appeared in the seventh volume (1812).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-candidissimus: Narcissus candidissimus, the white daffodil, drawn from a bulb of the Narcisse family with strap-shaped leaves and a pale flower above. The plate was issued in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), a stipple engraving printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-dubius: Narcissus dubius, the doubtful daffodil, named by Gouan for the difficulty of separating it from the white-flowered forms of Narcissus tazetta, here showing three to six snow-white blooms above glaucous linear leaves. Redoute drew it for the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-gouani: Narcissus gouani, Gouan's daffodil, a single fragrant flower on a sword-shaped scape, its pale-yellow funnel perianth set off by a deeper orange-yellow cup with crenate wavy margins. From the family of Narcisses in Jussieu's system; the dissection figures below enlarge the flower's sexual parts after the botanical convention of the day.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-intermedius: Narcissus intermedius, named for standing between the jonquil and the scented daffodils, carrying one to four fragrant yellow flowers above channelled dark-green leaves. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814); the crown sits about four times shorter than the spreading perianth segments.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-jonquilla: Narcissus jonquilla, the jonquil, recognisable by its rush-like semi-cylindrical leaves and short bell-shaped cup, with two to seven small sweetly scented flowers turned to one side. The botanical text supplied with Redoute's plates notes its leaves resemble those of the rushes, the source of its name; this plate came in the third volume (1805).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-laetus: Narcissus laetus, the glad daffodil, long confused with the scented narcissus it closely resembles, separated by Salisbury for its smaller flower and a crown cut rather than left whole. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814), a stipple engraving printed in colour and hand-finished.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-minor: Narcissus minor, the lesser daffodil, a single flower on a short scape above glaucous snowdrop-like leaves, its inner crown cylindrical and frilled with six wavy lobes. From the Narcisse family in Jussieu's classification; the enlarged stamen and seed figures below follow the period's botanical convention.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-odorus: Narcissus odorus, the scented daffodil, set apart by a bell-shaped cup half the length of the perianth lobes and divided into six rounded segments, carrying one to three yellow flowers twice the size of the tazetta's. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-poeticus: Narcissus poeticus, the poet's narcissus, a single nodding white flower on a flattened scape, its very short lemon-yellow cup crenate and rimmed with red. The plate notes some forms carry a scarlet margin and others an orange or near-yellow one; Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-pseudo-narcissu: Narcissus pseudo-narcissus, the wild daffodil, its trumpet flower rising on a single scape above strap-shaped leaves from a tunicate bulb. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the stipple engraving was printed in colour from one plate and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-narcissus-pumilus: Narcissus pumilus, the dwarf daffodil, here described as a small undescribed garden species, a solitary small white flower on a short flattened scape above few glaucous linear leaves. De Candolle and others supplied the text accompanying Redoute's plates; this one appeared in the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-radiatus: Narcissus radiatus, a rounded bulb giving linear grooved leaves and a smooth scape ending in two flowers, the six oval-pointed segments spread wheel-like around a very short crenate cup. From the Narcisse family in Jussieu's system; Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-tazetta: Narcissus tazetta, the bunch-flowered daffodil, two or three scapes from one bulb each carrying three to eight flowers above broad green leaves, with a cylindrical tube and six spreading segments around a yellow cup. The text records white and yellow-cupped variants beside the form shown; this plate opened the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-narcissus-tenuifolius: Narcissus tenuifolius, the slender-leaved daffodil, close to the hoop-petticoat but smaller throughout, a single golden scentless flower above thread-like dark-green leaves with a protruding style. From the Narcisse family in Jussieu's classification; Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-neottia-elata: Neottia elata, a tall slender orchid bearing a one-sided spike of small greenish flowers above oval half-fleshy leaves, the lip pale yellow-green with a faint rose tint. From the orchid family in Jussieu's system; the enlarged figures below detail the column and its sexual parts after the convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-neottia-speciosa: Neottia speciosa, an orchid with fusiform tubers and oval-lanceolate leaves giving a tall reddish stem topped by a raceme of rose-pink flowers, set among pale-rose bracts of the same colour. From the orchid family in Jussieu's classification; Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-ophiostachys-virginica: Ophiostachys virginica, a dioecious plant with a rosette of elliptic basal leaves and a tall stem ending in a single yellowish-white raceme, the male spikes likened to those of weld. The plate places it in the Colchicaceae of the Flore Francaise; Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-ophrys-lilifolia: Ophrys lilifolia, the lily-leaved orchid, two oval keeled basal leaves and a bare scape carrying a loose raceme of about twenty-five flowers, the outer segments greenish-violet and the broad lip pale violet. From the orchid family in Jussieu's system; the dissection figures below enlarge the column and anther after the day's botanical convention.
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-arabicum: Ornithogalum arabicum, the Arabian star-of-Bethlehem, a tall cylindrical scape carrying a short corymb-like raceme of broad white bell-shaped flowers, each centred on a glossy near-black ovary. The text calls this contrast its true distinguishing mark; Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-aureum: Ornithogalum aureum, the golden star-of-Bethlehem, a cylindrical scape bearing a crowded raceme of orange-yellow flowers, the six segments striped lengthwise and green at the base beneath. From the asphodel family in Jussieu's classification; Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-fistulosum: Ornithogalum fistulosum, its slender thread-like basal leaves hollow within, rising from a small ovoid bulb to scattered yellow six-parted flowers on hairy pedicels. The Asphodel-family plant carries enlarged stamen figures at the foot of the sheet, drawn for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-lacteum: Ornithogalum lacteum, its strap-shaped fleshy leaves below a dense raceme of milk-white flowers that open from a cone into a near-cylinder. Each segment carries a small green basal spot, and the stamens run half the length of the perianth. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-longibractea: Ornithogalum longibracteatum, recognised by its huge apple-sized bulb sitting half above the soil, with a tall scape carrying a long raceme of white flowers each crossed by a broad green stripe. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method Redoute used across all eight folio volumes.
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-luteum: Ornithogalum luteum, growing from a hazelnut-sized bulb to a single channelled leaf and a terminal umbel of three to seven yellow flowers, green on the outside. A collar of opposite bracts sits below the blooms, with stamen and ovary figures enlarged at the foot. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-minimum: Ornithogalum minimum, a dwarf species with a flexuous stem often lying on the ground, two narrow leaves, and a small corymb of six to ten star-shaped flowers, bright yellow within. The Asphodel-family plant shows enlarged dissection figures below, a botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-nutans: Ornithogalum nutans, its channelled basal leaves matching the scape, which ends in a one-sided raceme of six to twelve greenish flowers that spread then droop. The broad membranous filaments and the three-valved seed capsule appear in figures at the foot. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-pyramidale: Ornithogalum pyramidale, its drooping pale-green leaves below a tall scape bearing a conical raceme of flowers, white within and green outside with white margins. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, here for the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-pyrenaicum: Ornithogalum pyrenaicum, the Pyrenean star-of-Bethlehem, with a slender leafless scape carrying a long spike of small greenish-yellow flowers. Redoute drew this Asphodel-family species for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), the plates printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-spathaceum: Ornithogalum spathaceum, distinguished from its yellow umbel-flowered kin by a slender scape, thread-like basal leaves, and a single spathe-like leaf rising on the stem to the level of the smaller flowers. Long confused with related species, it grows from a pea-sized bulb. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-tenuifolium: Ornithogalum tenuifolium, its narrow awl-shaped dark-green leaves rising with the bare scape to a short dense raceme of eight to twelve flowers, white with a broad green midrib stripe. Redoute drew this Asphodel-family species for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811); the enlarged stamen figures below follow period convention.
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-thyrsoides: Ornithogalum thyrsoides, its channelled pale-green leaves below a bare scape ending in a dense raceme that lengthens during flowering, the white segments marked with a small green basal spot. The botanist A.P. de Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text that ran with Redoute's plates in Les Liliacees.
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-trigynum: Ornithogalum trigynum, growing from an apricot-sized bulb to soft trailing leaves and a long cylindrical raceme of many flowers, whitish above and pale green beneath. Unusually for the group it has three styles, reflected in its Linnaean class on the plate. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-ornithogalum-umbellatum: Ornithogalum umbellatum, the common star-of-Bethlehem, its narrow channelled leaves below a scape of white flowers banded green on the reverse and arranged in a loose false umbel. The six-angled three-celled capsule appears in a figure at the foot. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-amboinense: Pancratium amboinense, unusual in the genus for its broad heart-based stalked leaves rather than strap-like ones, with a scape carrying an umbel of about a dozen small white flowers in a two-valved spathe. This Amaryllis-family species was drawn for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-calathiforme: Pancratium calathiforme, set apart by its large nectary cup and the arrangement of the stamens, with linear leaves in two ranks and a flattened two-edged scape bearing two stalkless white flowers. The Amaryllis-family plant shows its long green perianth tube and dissection figures, drawn for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-croceum: Pancratium croceum, distinct among the genus for its saffron-yellow flowers rather than white, borne in a nodding umbel from a split three-valved spathe atop a glaucous scape. The stamen filaments are joined by a toothed membrane into a cylindrical cup. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-declinatum-358: Pancratium declinatum, its dark-green strap-shaped leaves below a strongly flattened two-edged scape carrying an umbel of about ten large stalkless white flowers. An inverted-cone nectary joins the stamen filaments, shown enlarged at the foot. Redoute drew this version for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-declinatum-414: Pancratium declinatum, here flowering nearly year-round with twelve to twenty faintly fragrant white flowers in a terminal umbel above broad pointed leaves. A funnel-shaped nectary with twelve teeth unites the awl-shaped filaments. This second plate of the species appeared in the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-disciforme: Pancratium disciforme, named for the flared membrane joining the stamen filaments, which spreads almost into a disc, above linear leaves and a scape of three white flowers in a short spathe. The Amaryllis-family plant shows its long perianth tube and orange-yellow pollen in figures below, drawn for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-fragrans: Pancratium fragrans, with about a dozen bright-green tapering stalked leaves and a flattened two-edged scape bearing four to six stalkless white flowers, the limb cut into narrow channelled segments. A funnel-shaped six-toothed nectary unites the stamens. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-illyricum: Pancratium illyricum, its two-ranked blunt leaves below a flattened scape bearing an umbel of seven or eight nearly stalkless white flowers from a membranous spathe. The crown between the filaments opens star-like and splits into two-pointed lobes, a feature unique to this species. Drawn for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-littorale: Pancratium littorale, with two-ranked pointed leaves and a flattened scape carrying five or six large faintly scented white flowers in an umbel. The bell-shaped membrane joining the long divergent filaments has nearly entire margins, distinguishing it within the genus. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-maritimum: Pancratium maritimum, the sea daffodil, its glaucous strap-like leaves in two ranks below a scape of fragrant white flowers, the limb cut into six pointed segments above a funnel-shaped nectary. The pistil and three-angled ovary appear in figures at the foot. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-parviflorum: Pancratium parviflorum, with pale-green channelled leaves and a flattened two-edged scape bearing six small star-opening flowers, the white segments marked by a broad green stripe outside. This small-flowered Amaryllis-family species closed out the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-pancratium-speciosum-156: Pancratium speciosum, an umbel of large white flowers above broad lanceolate leaves, the stamens joined by a bell-shaped petal-like membrane bearing sharp teeth between the filaments. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805). The enlarged stamen and pistil figures below follow the botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-pancratium-speciosum-412: Pancratium speciosum, its numerous white flowers cut nearly to the green tube into six narrow recurved lobes, set above dark green ovate-lanceolate leaves on a sharply flattened scape. This plate appeared in the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812). The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-paris-quadrifolia: Paris quadrifolia, a slender stem topped by four whorled ovate leaves and a single greenish flower whose eight narrow segments stand in two ranks. The plate, from the fourth volume (1807), notes the black rounded ovary that ripens into a dark berry. Redoute placed the genus in the asparagus family on the Jussieu line.
redoute-lilies-peliosanthes-teta: Peliosanthes teta, its lance-shaped strongly veined leaves rising from thick fibrous roots, with a long raceme of small bluish flowers clustered in groups of four or five along the scape. The funnel-shaped perianth has a transverse hexagonal partition across the tube's mouth. The plate appeared in the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-peronia-stricta: Peronia stricta, a tall slender stem nearly two metres high carrying large ovate leaves on long sheathing petioles, the scentless flowers gathered in a compound spike with leafy bracts. The work places it in the canna family on the Jussieu line. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-phalangium-bicolor: Phalangium bicolor, its grassy basal leaves below a branched panicle of six-parted flowers that are rose-violet outside and white within. The plate, from the fourth volume (1807), records the woolly-haired filaments and the spherical three-celled capsule. Redoute placed the genus among the asphodels on the Jussieu line.
redoute-lilies-phalangium-elatum: Phalangium elatum, a slender-stemmed member of the asphodel group with narrow basal leaves and a branched spray of small six-parted flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807). The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-phalangium-liliago: Phalangium liliago, narrow keeled leaves below a tall simple scape ending in an elongated raceme of pure white flowers, each cut to the base into six three-nerved segments. The plate dates to the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809). The enlarged stamen and ovary figures below follow the botanical convention of the day.
redoute-lilies-phalangium-liliastrum: Phalangium liliastrum, the St Bruno's lily, its few large bell-shaped white flowers turned mostly to one side on a leafless scape, the stamens curving toward the lower side of the flower. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809). The botanist A.P. de Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text.
redoute-lilies-phalangium-pendulum: Phalangium pendulum, slender branching stems carrying loose racemes of tiny nodding flowers grouped in threes, the outer segments violet and the inner ones edged in white. The plate, from the sixth volume (1811), records the bearded filaments and citron-yellow anthers. Redoute placed the genus among the asphodels.
redoute-lilies-phalangium-ramosum: Phalangium ramosum, fleshy white roots spread like spider's legs below a branched scape carrying a loose pyramidal panicle of white wheel-shaped flowers. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809). The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-phalangium-serotinum: Phalangium serotinum, a slender bulb sending up two narrow leaves and a scape topped by one large flower whose six spreading segments are yellow at the base, white within and reddish outside. The plate, from the fifth volume (1809), notes the top-shaped three-celled capsule. Redoute placed the genus among the asphodels.
redoute-lilies-phormium-tenax: Phormium tenax, the New Zealand flax, its tough sword-shaped leaves spread fan-wise like an iris below a tall branched flowering stem reaching two metres. The leaves split lengthwise into strong fibres, their margins cartilaginous and orange-red. Redoute drew it for the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-pitcairnia-angustifolia: Pitcairnia angustifolia, its narrow stiff leaves rising in a tuft and edged the whole length with brown horny spines, below a loose raceme on a woolly stem. The work places it in the pineapple family on the Jussieu line. The plate appeared in the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-pitcairnia-bromeliaefolia: Pitcairnia bromeliaefolia, a tuft of leaves spined with short hooked teeth only on the lower half, below a simple loose raceme of flowers on short bracted pedicels. The work places the genus in the pineapple family on the Jussieu line. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-pitcairnia-latifolia: Pitcairnia latifolia, broad lanceolate leaves spined only near the base below a firm white-downy stem carrying a dense cylindrical spike of crowded red flowers. The plate, from the second volume (1804), places the genus in the pineapple family. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-pleea-tenuifolia: Pleea tenuifolia, slender sword-shaped basal leaves below upright stems bearing a few fairly large flowers, each perianth tawny-yellow and cut to the base into six lanceolate segments that persist around the ripening fruit. The work places it in the rush family on the Jussieu line. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-polianthes-tuberosa: Polianthes tuberosa, the tuberose, a tall firm stem carrying alternate linear leaves and a long spike of fragrant white funnel-shaped flowers, often paired and wrapped in spathes. The work places the genus in the narcissus family on the Jussieu line. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-polygonatum-latifolium: Polygonatum latifolium, a flexuous stem with broad alternate leaves hairy beneath along the veins, the white green-lined flowers hanging from branched axillary stalks. The plate, from the fifth volume (1809), records the spherical blue-black three-celled berry. Redoute placed the genus in the asparagus family on the Jussieu line.
redoute-lilies-polygonatum-multiflorum: Polygonatum multiflorum, an arching cylindrical stem with alternate clasping leaves and clusters of pendulous white tubular flowers tipped with six short green teeth. The plate, from the fourth volume (1807), notes the pea-sized blue-black berry. Redoute drew it among the asparagus family on the Jussieu line.
redoute-lilies-polygonatum-sibiricum: Polygonatum sibiricum, an angular stem with narrow whorled leaves hooked at the tips, the small greenish-white flowers on forked stalks ringed by two opposite bracts at the division. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811). The enlarged floral figures below follow the botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-polygonatum-verticillatum: Polygonatum verticillatum, a slender stem set with crowded whorls of five or six lanceolate-linear leaves, the small whitish pendulous flowers borne from the middle and lower whorls. The plate, from the fifth volume (1809), records the round violet three-celled berry. The genus sits in the asparagus family on the Jussieu line.
redoute-lilies-polygonatum-vulgare: Polygonatum vulgare, Solomon's seal, a strongly angled stem with eight to ten ovate leaves and solitary or paired white pendulous flowers on arched axillary stalks. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809). The dissection figures at the foot of the sheet show the flower's parts enlarged.
redoute-lilies-pontederia-cordata: Pontederia cordata, an aquatic plant of still waters with long-petioled heart-shaped leaves and a spike of blue almost two-lipped flowers held above the surface. The text notes a variety gathered by Fraser in South Carolina. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-sagittaria-ovata: Plate 411 shows Sagittaria ovata, its long-stalked oval leaves rising from the water beneath a loose pyramidal panicle of three-whorled monoecious flowers, male blooms above and female below. The classification line places it in the Alismataceae, the water-plantain family.
redoute-lilies-sagittaria-sagittifolia: Sagittaria sagittifolia, the common arrowhead, with its triangular arrow-shaped leaves on stout air-filled petioles and a simple terminal raceme of whorled flowers. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809); the lower stalks usually stand submerged in water.
redoute-lilies-sanseviera-carnea: Sanseviera carnea, its two-ranked linear-lanceolate leaves rising from a horizontal rhizome to a loose spike of pink flowers, each tubular bloom opening into six recurved segments. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811), placed by Jussieu among the asparagus family.
redoute-lilies-sanseviera-guineensis: Plate 330 shows Sanseviera guineensis, the bow-string hemp of Guinea, with stiff dark-banded leaves and a green scape bearing a dense raceme of white tubular flowers paired along its length. The dissection figures at the foot enlarge the stamens and floral parts, a botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-sanseviera-zeylanica: Sanseviera zeylanica, the Ceylon bow-string hemp, with fleshy channelled leaves marked by transverse bands and a thick scape carrying a crowded raceme of greenish-white flowers in clusters of four or five. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-scilla-amoena-130: Scilla amoena, with channelled basal leaves and angular scapes each ending in one to three amethyst-blue flowers larger than those of other squills. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the enlarged stamen and pistil figures below follow the period's botanical convention.
redoute-lilies-scilla-amoena-298: Plate 298 shows Scilla amoena again, an ovoid bulb sending up channelled leaves and slender scapes bearing four to six pale-blue flowers in a loose raceme, each segment marked with two whitish spots at the base. Jussieu's line places it among the Asphodels.
redoute-lilies-scilla-autumnalis: Scilla autumnalis, the autumn squill, with narrow almost thread-like leaves and slender scapes carrying a loose raceme of pale-blue or rosy flowers, the dissection figures showing ovary, capsule and black seeds. The plate appeared in the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-scilla-bifolia: Scilla bifolia, the two-leaved squill, with a pair of opposite sheathing leaves and a short terminal raceme of blue flowers whose perianth splits to the base into six spreading segments. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, and many specimens for the work were grown at Malmaison.
redoute-lilies-scilla-campanulata: Plate 435 shows Scilla campanulata, the bell-flowered squill, its lanceolate arching leaves below a slightly conical raceme of twelve to twenty pale-blue bell-shaped flowers, each pedicel set with two coloured bracts. It appeared in the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-scilla-italica: Scilla italica, the Italian squill, with soft linear keeled leaves and a short crowded terminal raceme of small pale greyish-blue flowers, each carried on a stout pedicel with a membranous bract. The descriptive text was supplied by A.P. de Candolle and the botanists who accompanied Redoute's plates.
redoute-lilies-scilla-lilio-hyacinthus: Scilla lilio-hyacinthus, notable for a scaly fleshy bulb resembling that of a true lily, with bright-green oblong leaves and a slender scape ending in five or six soft-blue flowers. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the fruit is a three-angled capsule.
redoute-lilies-scilla-lingulata: Scilla lingulata, distinguished by bracts split lengthwise into two or three linear shreds, with reflexed lanceolate leaves and a fairly tight raceme of blue flowers. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811), placed by Jussieu among the asphodels.
redoute-lilies-scilla-maritima: Plate 116 shows Scilla maritima, the sea squill, recognised by its spherical bulb larger than a fist that often sits half out of the ground, sending up a tall scape with a long raceme of white star-opening flowers. Its bracts carry a basal appendage found in no other squill.
redoute-lilies-scilla-non-scripta: Scilla non-scripta, the English bluebell, with linear basal leaves and an arched scape ending in a short one-sided nodding raceme of fragrant blue bell-shaped flowers. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-scilla-obtusifolia: Scilla obtusifolia, a blunt-leaved squill of the asphodel group, drawn with its bulb, basal leaves and raceme of blue flowers. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), the stipple engraving printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-scilla-patula: Scilla patula, the spreading squill, with broad leaves lying on the ground and an upright ovoid raceme of blue bell-shaped flowers that nod once fully open, each pedicel set with two awl-shaped blue bracts. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-scilla-peruviana: Plate 167 shows Scilla peruviana, with linear leaves spread in a wide rosette and a stout scape ending in a dense conical raceme of many blue-violet flowers. The lower dissection figures show the stamens and the three-angled, three-celled capsule typical of the squills.
redoute-lilies-scilla-pomeridiana: Scilla pomeridiana, with a thick fibrous-coated bulb and lanceolate leaves dotted with countless fine white points, the branching stem carrying widely spaced flowers along divergent limbs. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814), placed by Jussieu among the asphodels.
